scenarios.title: What the machine can do
scenarios.situation: A student argues that because a Turing machine is just a tape and a head, it cannot possibly run a web browser. A classmate counters that any modern computer is, in principle, a Turing machine with finite memory.
evidence: Turing described an abstract machine: an infinite tape, a read/write head, and a finite state table. He then showed a single 'universal' machine can simulate any other — the theoretical ancestor of the stored-program computer.
choices: The classmate is right: a universal Turing machine can simulate any computable process, so a web browser is computable in principle; only finite memory and speed separate the abstraction from hardware.
The student is right: a Turing machine can only do arithmetic, so complex software like browsers needs a fundamentally different model of computation.
Both are wrong: the universal machine result applies only to analog computers, not digital ones.
Neither matters: Turing machines were disproved by the discovery of undecidable problems.
scenarios.why: Universality is the point: one fixed machine design can carry out any computation any other can, given enough tape and time. Finite memory is a practical limitation, not a theoretical one.
scenarios.hint: What did Turing prove the universal machine could simulate?

scenarios.title: Setting up the imitation game
scenarios.situation: A startup claims its chatbot 'passes the Turing test' because 60% of users in an open chat said it seemed human. Their test had no time limit, no control comparison with a human, and users knew they were talking to a bot.
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest methodological objection, faithful to Turing's 1950 proposal?
evidence: Turing proposed the imitation game: an interrogator converses by text with a hidden human and a hidden machine, and tries to tell which is which. The machine passes if it fools the interrogator as often as a human fools them — a comparative, blinded setup.
choices: The test lacks the blinded comparison Turing specified — knowing the subject is a bot and having no human baseline means the 60% figure measures user credulity, not machine performance.
The test is invalid because Turing required the interrogator to be a computer scientist, which these users were not.
The test is invalid because 60% is below the 70% threshold Turing set for passing.
There is no objection: any conversation in which a majority judges the bot human counts as passing.
scenarios.why: Turing's game is a controlled comparison: blinded interrogator, text channel, machine versus human baseline. Without blinding and a baseline, the number is meaningless.
scenarios.hint: What two structural features make the imitation game a fair test?

scenarios.title: The universal bug detector
scenarios.situation: A vendor pitches a static-analysis tool that, for ANY program and ANY input, decides in finite time whether the program will terminate. The sales deck cites 'advances in formal methods' and offers a money-back guarantee.
scenarios.prompt: How should an engineer evaluate this claim?
evidence: Turing proved in 1936 that no general algorithm can decide, for every program-input pair, whether the program halts. Any claimed universal decider must fail on some input — the proof uses a diagonal argument: feed the decider a program built to do the opposite of what it predicts.
choices: Reject the universal claim: the halting problem is undecidable in general, so the tool must be restricted to a subclass of programs or use heuristics — ask which.
Accept it: modern SMT solvers have solved the halting problem for all practical programs.
Accept it conditionally: the tool works for all programs as long as they are written in a memory-safe language.
Reject it because static analysis is too slow for production code, though the theory is sound.
scenarios.why: Undecidability is a mathematical limit, not an engineering gap: no tool can decide termination for all programs. Real tools succeed by restricting the domain or accepting incompleteness.
scenarios.hint: What does 'undecidable' mean for a vendor's universal claim?

scenarios.title: The letter that never is
scenarios.situation: You are reconstructing the Bombe attack on Enigma for a museum exhibit. A visitor asks why the cryptanalysts' job was easier than brute-forcing all rotor settings.
scenarios.prompt: Which fact about the Enigma machine made the Bombe's logical attack possible?
evidence: The Enigma's reflector guaranteed a letter could never encrypt to itself. Turing and Welchman's Bombe exploited this: a guessed plaintext ('crib') could be tested against rotor positions, and any position producing a self-encryption was impossible — rapidly ruling out most settings.
choices: No letter ever encrypts to itself, so a crib (guessed plaintext) lets the Bombe eliminate rotor positions that would require a self-encryption — a logical contradiction that prunes the search space enormously.
The Enigma rotors never moved, so each letter always used the same substitution and frequency analysis broke it directly.
The Germans reused the same daily key for months, so one broken message revealed all traffic.
The Enigma had only 26 possible settings, so brute force was trivial and no cleverness was needed.
scenarios.why: The reflector's no-self-encryption property turns a crib into a contradiction engine: wrong settings announce themselves. That is cryptanalysis — exploiting structure, not just trying keys.
scenarios.hint: How does a true statement about the cipher become a search shortcut?

scenarios.title: Diagonalization in practice
scenarios.situation: A junior engineer proposes: 'Run the claimed halting-decider H on a new program P that asks H whether P halts on its own source, then does the opposite.' The team lead says this is just a trick, not a proof.
scenarios.prompt: Is the 'trick' a valid refutation, and why?
choices: Yes — it is the diagonal argument: if H existed and were correct, P creates a contradiction either way (H says halts, P loops; H says loops, P halts), so no such H can exist. The 'trick' is the proof.
No — P is an illegal self-referential program, and real deciders are only required to work on well-formed, non-self-referential code.
No — the argument only works for programs written before 1936; modern languages escape it.
Yes, but only probabilistically: it shows H must be wrong on at least half of all inputs.
scenarios.why: Self-reference is legitimate input. The diagonal construction shows any candidate decider fails on at least one program — itself. That single counterexample is enough to kill the universal claim.
scenarios.hint: If H were perfect, what happens when it meets a program designed to disobey it?

scenarios.title: Spots from nowhere
scenarios.situation: A biology student reads Turing's 1952 paper 'The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis' and is surprised: a computer scientist writing about how leopards get their spots. She wonders what computation has to do with embryos.
scenarios.prompt: What is the core idea of Turing's reaction-diffusion model?
evidence: Turing showed that two chemicals — an activator and an inhibitor diffusing at different rates through tissue — can spontaneously form stable patterns (spots, stripes) from a uniform start, with no blueprint. Local rules plus diffusion produce global order.
choices: Simple local chemical rules — activation plus faster-diffusing inhibition — can self-organize into spots and stripes without any central plan; pattern emerges from the dynamics, not from a pre-drawn map.
Turing proved that DNA contains a literal image of the animal's coat pattern, which chemicals then print onto the skin.
Turing showed that embryonic development requires a Turing machine inside each cell executing a pattern program.
Turing argued that spots are random mutations with no underlying mechanism, and computation is irrelevant.
scenarios.why: Reaction-diffusion is emergence made rigorous: uniform ingredients, local interactions, and different diffusion rates are enough to break symmetry and make pattern. It reframed development as a dynamical system.
scenarios.hint: Can global order appear with no one drawing the map?

scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Alan Turing?

Restart all components — Alan Turing issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately

domains.name: The Turing Machine

scenarios.title: Trace the Machine
scenarios.situation: A Turing machine has rules: (q0,1)->(1,R,q0); (q0,0)->(0,R,q0); (q0,blank)->(blank,L,q1); (q1,1)->(0,L,q1); (q1,0)->(1,S,qH); (q1,blank)->(1,S,qH). Tape: 1 0, head on the leftmost 1.
scenarios.prompt: What is on the tape when it halts?
choices: 1 1 — the machine halts with tape reading '11'.
1 0 0 — it appends a zero.
1 1 0 — carry propagates wrongly.
It never halts — the rules loop.
scenarios.why: The correct approach traces mechanically: q0 scans right past 1,0 to blank, enters q1 moving left; q1 sees 0, writes 1, halts. Tape: 1 1. This is the binary incrementer on input '10' (2 -> 3).
scenarios.hint: Follow the head: which state, which symbol, which rule — step by step.

scenarios.title: Design Decision
scenarios.situation: You must design a Turing machine that decides whether a binary string is a palindrome (reads the same forward and backward).
scenarios.prompt: What is the essential design idea?
choices: One state is enough — just compare ends directly.
Count the characters first, then compare halves.
Mark-and-compare: mark the leftmost unmarked symbol, remember it in the state, scan to the rightmost unmarked symbol and check equality, repeat inward. States encode 'what I'm looking for.'
Palindromes are undecidable — no machine can do this.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses states as memory: the finite control remembers the left symbol while the head travels right. Marking symbols tracks progress. Palindromes are easily decidable — the challenge is only the design.
scenarios.hint: How can a finite-state control 'remember' a symbol across the tape?

scenarios.title: Why One Machine Runs Everything
scenarios.situation: A student asks: 'If a universal machine can simulate any machine, why do we have different computers and languages at all?'
choices: We don't need them — one computer design would suffice.
Universality is theoretical and doesn't apply to real computers.

Universality is about what CAN be computed, not how fast or conveniently. Different machines and languages exist for speed, cost, and human usability — simulation overhead is real, and humans need expressive tools.
Universal machines can only simulate slow machines.
scenarios.why: The correct approach separates computability from practicality: the UTM proves one machine suffices in principle, but engineering cares about efficiency and humans care about expressiveness. Theory defines the boundary; practice optimizes within it.
scenarios.hint: Does 'can simulate' mean 'should simulate for everything'?
evidence: Why many computers if one universal machine exists?

scenarios.title: What Was the Paper For?
scenarios.situation: A colleague claims Turing's 1936 paper was 'the blueprint for building the first computer.'
choices: Nothing — that's exactly right.
The paper was about AI, not hardware.
Turing opposed building computers.

The paper was a logic paper answering the Entscheidungsproblem — it defined computation to prove a limit on decision procedures. The universal machine was a proof device; its hardware implications were recognized later.
scenarios.why: The correct approach keeps the history straight: 1936 was about Hilbert's decision problem, not engineering. The UTM-as-stored-program reading is retrospective insight, not the paper's purpose — and that distinction matters for understanding both.
scenarios.hint: What question was Turing actually hired (by logic) to answer?

scenarios.title: Finite Tape Objection
scenarios.situation: A skeptic: 'Real computers have finite memory, so the infinite tape makes the whole model irrelevant.'
choices: They're right — the model is useless.
Real computers are actually infinite.

The infinite tape is an idealization meaning 'no fixed bound': any finite computation uses finite tape, and results about the model apply to all sufficiently large machines. Finite-memory machines are a different, weaker class (finite automata) — the idealization is what gives the model its power.
Turing machines need infinite time too.
scenarios.why: The correct approach defends idealization properly: the infinite tape means memory isn't the limiting factor in the analysis — exactly like frictionless planes in physics. Every real computation fits in some finite portion.
scenarios.hint: What does 'infinite' idealize away — and why is that useful?

scenarios.title: Do Variants Add Power?
scenarios.situation: You're comparing Turing machine variants: multi-tape, nondeterministic, and two-dimensional tape machines.
scenarios.prompt: Which statement about their computational power is true?
choices: Multi-tape machines compute strictly more than single-tape machines.
Nondeterministic machines decide the halting problem.
Two-dimensional tapes are weaker than one-dimensional ones.
All are computationally equivalent to the basic model — they differ in convenience and speed, not in what they can compute. Robustness of the model is evidence for the Church-Turing thesis.
scenarios.why: The correct approach knows the robustness results: every reasonable variant simulates and is simulated by the basic machine. This insensitivity to details is exactly why the model captures 'computation' rather than one machine design.
scenarios.hint: If details don't change the power, what does that suggest?

scenarios.title: Where the Model Lives Today
scenarios.situation: A colleague dismisses Turing machines as purely historical, with no relevance to modern practice.
scenarios.prompt: Where does the model DIRECTLY appear in modern practice?
choices: In CPU clock speeds.

In interpreters, virtual machines, and emulators — each is a universal machine simulating another: exactly Turing's 1936 construction, engineered. Complexity theory also uses the model to define P, NP, and hardness.
Only in academic papers.
Nowhere — it's purely historical.
scenarios.why: The correct approach sees the UTM in daily engineering: every interpreter and VM is a universal machine. And complexity theory's hardest questions (P vs NP) are phrased in Turing machine terms — the model is working infrastructure, not museum piece.
scenarios.hint: What is an interpreter, formally?

domains.name: Computability Theory

scenarios.title: The Perfect Antivirus
scenarios.situation: A startup claims their AI detects ALL malware with zero false negatives — a perfect virus detector.
choices: AI isn't good enough yet — give it time.
It needs more training data.

Malware detection is behavioral: 'is this program malicious?' is a nontrivial semantic property, undecidable by Rice's theorem (via halting). Perfect detection is impossible in principle — sell heuristics, never perfection.
Regulators won't allow it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach applies Rice's theorem: maliciousness is a semantic property of programs, so no decider exists — this is a mathematical impossibility, not an engineering gap. The honest product is heuristic detection with measured rates.
scenarios.hint: Is this a hard problem or an impossible one?
evidence: Perfect malware detection, zero false negatives

scenarios.title: The Uncountable Programs
scenarios.situation: Someone argues: 'Programs are finite strings, so there are countably many — therefore every language of programs is decidable.'
choices: Programs aren't finite strings.

Countability of programs doesn't imply decidability of their properties: there are countably many programs but uncountably many languages, and diagonalization shows specific ones (like HALT) undecidable. Enumeration isn't decision.
Some languages aren't made of programs.
Finite strings can't be listed.
scenarios.why: The correct approach separates listing from deciding: you can enumerate all programs and still be unable to decide a property of them. Diagonalization exploits exactly this — the diagonal machine is in the enumeration but defeats the decider.
scenarios.hint: Does 'I can list them all' imply 'I can decide everything about them'?

scenarios.title: Reduction Direction
scenarios.situation: You want to prove L = 'does program P output the string hello?' is undecidable, given that HALT is undecidable.
choices: Reduce L to HALT: show deciding HALT would decide L.
Show L is a subset of HALT.
Enumerate all programs that output hello.
Reduce HALT to L: assume a decider for L, then decide HALT(P,x) by building Q that runs P(x) and outputs hello iff P halts — so an L-decider yields a HALT-decider, contradiction.
scenarios.why: The correct approach reduces FROM the known-undecidable problem TO the target: 'if I could decide L, I could decide HALT.' The construction (Q runs P, then prints hello) is computable, completing the proof.
scenarios.hint: Which direction proves L hard — HALT-to-L or L-to-HALT?

scenarios.title: Decidable or Not?
scenarios.situation: Consider the language: { (P, x) : P halts on x within 1000 steps }.
choices: Yes — decidable: simulate P on x for at most 1000 steps and answer. Bounded resources make it decidable; unbounded 'ever halts' is what defeats deciders.
No — it's the halting problem.
Recognizable but not decidable.
Undecidable by Rice's theorem.
scenarios.why: The correct approach notices the bound: 1000 steps is finite, so simulation always terminates with an answer. Undecidability needs the unbounded quantifier — bounds restore decidability. This is why timeouts are the practical escape hatch.
scenarios.hint: What changes when you add 'within 1000 steps'?

scenarios.title: Find the Flaw
scenarios.situation: A 'proof' claims: 'H exists. Run H(P,x). If it says halts, we halt. So H works.' Your colleague is convinced.
choices: The proof is actually correct.
H might be slow.

The argument assumes H's verdict is correct without justification — it describes USING a halting decider, not constructing one. The real proof must show no such H can exist (via the diagonal D); this 'proof' begs the question.
D is not a valid program.
scenarios.why: The correct approach spots circularity: the argument presupposes the decider it claims to establish. Genuine undecidability proofs derive contradiction from the assumption — they don't restate it.
scenarios.hint: Does this argument construct H or merely assume it?

scenarios.title: Recognizable but Not Decidable
scenarios.situation: Consider the halting language HALT = {(P,x) : P halts on x}.
choices: Decidable — just run it.
Not even recognizable.
Finite — only finitely many halting programs exist.
Recognizable but not decidable: simulate P on x — if it halts, say yes (recognition). But no machine halts with yes/no on ALL inputs (Turing's proof). The asymmetry is the point.
scenarios.why: The correct approach holds both halves: the simulator recognizes (confirms yes-instances), while the diagonal proof kills decidability. This asymmetry — confirming vs ruling out — is the heart of computability theory.
scenarios.hint: Can you confirm yes-instances? Can you rule out no-instances?

scenarios.title: The Linter That Catches Everything
scenarios.situation: Your team wants a CI check that rejects any commit containing an infinite loop. Guaranteed.
choices: Build it — loops are easy to spot.

Ship it with a timeout and document the limits: perfect loop detection is the halting problem (undecidable), so guarantee 'catches many' not 'catches all.' Timeouts, restricted patterns, and heuristics are the honest tools.
It's impossible, so do no checking at all.
Only check Python, not other languages.
scenarios.why: The correct approach translates theory into product honesty: undecidability forbids perfection, not usefulness. Bounded execution (timeouts) plus pattern heuristics catches the practical cases — sell that, not certainty.
scenarios.hint: What CAN you guarantee here?
evidence: CI check guaranteeing no infinite loops

domains.name: Church, Turing, and the Thesis

scenarios.title: Equivalent Means What?
scenarios.situation: A student: 'If lambda calculus and Turing machines are equivalent, I can use them interchangeably for everything, right?'
choices: Yes — identical in every respect.

Equivalent in COMPUTABILITY (same functions computable), not in convenience or efficiency: choose machines for step-counting and lower bounds, lambda for language semantics and type theory. Same boundary, different tools.
No — they're completely different.
Equivalent only for simple programs.
scenarios.why: The correct approach scopes 'equivalent' precisely: same class of computable functions, different strengths as proof tools. Interchangeable for what-can-be-computed questions; not interchangeable for how-fast or how-expressive questions.
scenarios.hint: Equivalent with respect to WHAT property?

scenarios.title: Can the Thesis Be Proved?
scenarios.situation: A philosopher demands a formal proof of the Church-Turing thesis.
choices: Gödel proved it in 1931.
It can — mathematicians are just lazy.
It's too obviously true to need proof.

The thesis links a FORMAL notion (Turing-computable) to an INFORMAL one ('effectively calculable') — proof needs both sides formalized, which would presuppose the answer. Evidence (model convergence, no counterexamples) is the appropriate support.
scenarios.why: The correct approach sees the epistemological point: you can't formally prove a claim about an informal concept. The thesis earns trust the way physical laws do — through survived challenges, not derivation.
scenarios.hint: What would a proof need that it can't have?

scenarios.title: Reduce It
scenarios.situation: Beta-reduce: (λx.λy.x) P Q, where P and Q are arbitrary terms.
choices: (λx.λy.x) P Q -> P — apply outer: substitute P for x gives λy.P; apply to Q: substitute Q for y (absent) gives P. This is TRUE selecting its first argument.
Q — it picks the second.
P Q — application distributes.
It doesn't reduce — stuck.
scenarios.why: The correct approach substitutes mechanically: (λx.λy.x) P -> λy.P (x:=P), then (λy.P) Q -> P (y absent, Q discarded). TRUE-as-function picks the first of two — booleans from pure functions.
scenarios.hint: Substitute step by step — what happens to Q?

scenarios.title: The Hypercomputer Startup
scenarios.situation: A startup claims a device solving the halting problem via 'real-number computation with infinite precision.' They seek investment.
choices: Invest — breakthrough opportunity.
The math checks out, so it must work.

Demand the physical mechanism: infinite-precision reals require infinite information storage and noiseless analog operations — physically impossible (thermal noise, quantum limits). Unfalsified math on unphysical assumptions isn't engineering.
Turing was wrong, so anything goes.
scenarios.why: The correct approach separates mathematical models from physical realizability: hypercomputation proofs always smuggle in an unphysical operation. The investment question is physics, not logic — and the physics says no.
scenarios.hint: What physical operation does the claim require?

scenarios.title: Does Quantum Break the Thesis?
scenarios.situation: Headline: 'Quantum computers break the limits Turing proved.'
choices: Quantum computers still can't decide the halting problem: they change EFFICIENCY (BQP vs P), not computability. Diagonalization works on quantum hardware too — no speedup defeats a proof of impossibility.
Quantum computers are just faster classical ones.
Turing never considered physics.
The headline is right — Turing's limits are obsolete.
scenarios.why: The correct approach keeps the two theses apart: Church-Turing (computability — stands) vs extended thesis (efficiency — challenged). The halting proof uses no assumption quantum violates.
scenarios.hint: Which thesis does quantum actually challenge?

scenarios.title: What 'Turing-Complete' Means
scenarios.situation: A job posting demands 'Turing-complete programming skills.' In an interview they ask what Turing-complete means.
choices: It means you know the Turing language.

A system is Turing-complete if it can simulate any Turing machine — i.e., it computes all computable functions (given unbounded memory). Most real languages are; the interesting question is usually expressiveness and ergonomics, not completeness.
It means AI-powered.
It means the fastest possible.
scenarios.why: The correct approach defines it operationally (universal simulation) and adds the practical footnote: completeness is a low bar most languages clear — plus the memory caveat, since real machines are finite.
scenarios.hint: Complete with respect to what — and with what caveat?

scenarios.title: Church's Own Result
scenarios.situation: It's 1936. Alonzo Church has just published his own attack on the Entscheidungsproblem — using lambda calculus, not machines.
scenarios.prompt: What did Church prove, and why does its independence from Turing's work matter?
choices: He was Turing's student.
He built the first computer.
He proved P != NP.

He proved the Entscheidungsproblem unsolvable via lambda calculus — independently of Turing. Two different formalisms, same verdict: the boundary is formalism-independent, which is the core evidence for the thesis.
scenarios.why: The correct approach credits the independence: Church (lambda calculus) and Turing (machines) converged on unsolvability from opposite directions. That convergence — not either proof alone — is why the thesis commands belief.
scenarios.hint: Why does independence strengthen the conclusion?

domains.name: Logic Foundations

scenarios.title: Which Dream Died When?
scenarios.situation: A student mixes up the history: 'Gödel proved computers can't decide everything in 1936.'
choices: Turing proved everything in 1936 alone.
Hilbert's program succeeded.
Close enough — the details don't matter.

Gödel (1931) killed completeness and provable consistency for arithmetic-strength systems; Turing/Church (1936) killed decidability of first-order logic. Different years, different theorems, different victims.
scenarios.why: The correct approach separates the kills: Gödel 1931 (incompleteness), Turing/Church 1936 (undecidability). Conflating them loses the causal story — Gödel's limits motivated Turing's definition of computation.
scenarios.hint: Who killed what, and when?
evidence: 'Gödel proved computers can't decide everything in 1936'

scenarios.title: What Counts as a Method?
scenarios.situation: Before 1936, mathematicians argued about whether a 'definite method' for logic existed — but couldn't settle it.
scenarios.prompt: Why was Turing's definition the breakthrough?
choices: You can't prove NO method exists until 'method' is defined precisely — Turing's machine turned an intuitive notion into a mathematical object, making impossibility PROVABLE. Definition enabled the negative result.
He asked Hilbert directly.
He built a faster method.
He proved the method existed.
scenarios.why: The correct approach sees the meta-move: the Entscheidungsproblem was unanswerable while 'method' was informal. Formalization didn't just help — it was the entire breakthrough, converting philosophy into mathematics.
scenarios.hint: Why couldn't anyone prove the negative before the definition?

scenarios.title: What Gödel Doesn't Say
scenarios.situation: A blogger writes: 'Gödel proved that truth is relative and science can't know anything for certain.'
choices: Only philosophers need Gödel.
The blogger is right — embrace uncertainty.

Gödel's theorems are precise claims about formal systems containing arithmetic: some arithmetical truths are unprovable in any fixed consistent system. They say nothing about 'truth being relative' or science in general.
Gödel proved math is inconsistent.
scenarios.why: The correct approach resists scope creep: the theorems have exact hypotheses (consistent, arithmetic-strength, formal). Popularizations that drop the hypotheses produce mysticism, not insight.
scenarios.hint: What are the theorem's actual hypotheses?

scenarios.title: Paradox or Theorem?
scenarios.situation: Someone objects: 'The Gödel sentence is just the liar paradox — this statement is false — dressed up. Paradoxes prove nothing.'
choices: They're right — it's just wordplay.

The liar paradox ('this statement is false') is semantically broken — neither true nor false. The Gödel sentence ('unprovable in F') is a well-formed arithmetical claim, TRUE (it is unprovable) but unprovable in F. Self-reference with content vs without.
Gödel sentences are false.
Paradoxes are more profound.
scenarios.why: The correct approach distinguishes vicious self-reference (liar: no stable truth value) from Gödel's (a genuine arithmetical statement via Gödel numbering, with a determinate truth value). One is a language bug; the other is a theorem.
scenarios.hint: Does the Gödel sentence have a truth value?

scenarios.title: Truth vs Provability
scenarios.situation: Two students argue: one says 'if it's true, it must be provable'; the other says 'provability is just a game with symbols.'
choices: Both — it's subjective.
The first — truth implies provability.
The second — provability is meaningless.

Neither, fully: Gödel showed truth outruns provability (true-but-unprovable sentences exist), yet provability isn't arbitrary — sound systems prove only truths. The concepts are related but distinct; confusing them is the original sin of this whole history.
scenarios.why: The correct approach holds the distinction: soundness (provable -> true) survives Gödel; completeness (true -> provable) doesn't, for strong systems. Truth is semantic, provability syntactic — related, not identical.
scenarios.hint: What does soundness guarantee that completeness doesn't?
evidence: 'True implies provable' vs 'provability is a game'

scenarios.title: Productive Failure
scenarios.situation: Historians call Hilbert's program 'the most productive failure in mathematics.'
scenarios.prompt: Why — what did the failure produce?
choices: It wasn't a failure at all.
Because Hilbert was famous.

Trying to secure mathematics FORCED the creation of proof theory, computability, and the formal definition of algorithm — the attempt's wreckage became computer science. The questions were better than the answers would have been.
Because Gödel was smarter.
scenarios.why: The correct approach values the questions: Hilbert's program organized logic for decades and its collapse produced the precise notion of computation. A successful program would have given us certainty; the failure gave us computers.
scenarios.hint: What did the ATTEMPT produce, regardless of outcome?

scenarios.title: The Decidable Fragment
scenarios.situation: Your team needs guaranteed-correct verification of hardware circuits. Full logic is undecidable — is the project doomed?
choices: Propositional logic (which suffices for combinational circuits) IS decidable — SAT solvers verify real chips daily. Undecidability hits first-order logic and beyond; pick the weakest logic that expresses your problem and inherit its good behavior.
Use machine learning instead.
Only verify small circuits.
Yes — undecidability kills all verification.
scenarios.why: The correct approach knows the map: limits are local to strong systems. Propositional logic is decidable (co-NP-complete, but practical via SAT), and hardware verification is its flagship success — billions of transistors verified, not doomed.
scenarios.hint: Which logic do circuits actually need?

domains.description: Hilbert's program, the Entscheidungsproblem, Gödel's theorems, and how logic's limits became computer science.

domains.name: AI Origins

scenarios.title: Design the Protocol
scenarios.situation: You're asked to run a rigorous modern imitation game. A colleague proposes: 'Let a chatbot talk to a judge for an hour, no human baseline.'
choices: The human baseline and time controls: without a human control, you can't calibrate judge accuracy; without time limits and misidentification-rate statistics, 'passing' is anecdote. Turing specified controls — they're what make it science.
A bigger chatbot.
More judges is all it needs.
Nothing — that's a solid test.
scenarios.why: The correct approach restores the controls: human baseline (judges misidentify humans too), fixed interaction time, and statistical misidentification rates. An uncontrolled demo measures vibes, not machine intelligence.
scenarios.hint: What turns a demo into an experiment?
evidence: Chatbot vs judge, 1 hour, no human control

scenarios.title: The Creativity Objection
scenarios.situation: A critic: 'Machines only do what they're told — Lady Lovelace proved they can never originate anything new.'
scenarios.prompt: Turing's reply, and its modern form?
choices: Turing agreed — machines can't create.
Machines clearly can — look at art generators.

Turing's reply: programmers are routinely SURPRISED by outputs (he gives examples), so 'never surprises' is false; and learning machines aren't 'told' in Lovelace's sense — they're educated. Origination vs surprise is still the live debate.
Lovelace was wrong about everything.
scenarios.why: The correct approach gives Turing's actual move: the surprise argument (we don't foresee all consequences of what we build) plus the learning-machine reframing. Modern generative models sharpen — not settle — the origination question.
scenarios.hint: Does 'not fully foreseen' equal 'originated'?

scenarios.title: Why Chess?
scenarios.situation: Turing built Turochamp — a chess program simulated by hand — in 1950, and early AI fixated on chess generally.
scenarios.prompt: Why chess? What made it the ideal laboratory?
choices: No other games existed.
Turing just liked board games.
Chess was commercially valuable.

Chess compresses reasoning into a clean lab: perfect information, clear win/loss, deep search, no robotics needed — it isolates 'thinking' from perception and motor control. Turochamp (hand-simulated, it beat one human) proved programs could play the reasoning game.
scenarios.why: The correct approach sees chess as drosophila — the model organism of early AI: reasoning isolated from embodiment. Turochamp matters as the first serious attempt to mechanize strategic thought, not as a strong player.
scenarios.hint: What does chess isolate that makes it a good lab?

scenarios.title: Program or Educate?
scenarios.situation: Two teams in 1950: Team A hand-codes adult-level rules; Team B builds a child machine and trains it.
scenarios.prompt: Who does Turing back, and why?
choices: Team A — explicit rules are reliable.

Team B: Turing argued programming adult intelligence directly was hopeless — too much to specify. The child machine (simple substrate + education + selection) was his bet, and six decades of ML vindicated the direction.
Neither — he thought AI impossible.
Both equally.
scenarios.why: The correct approach remembers the paper's second half: Turing explicitly proposed education over programming. The 'teacher ignorant of the inside' line predicts the interpretability problem 70 years early.
scenarios.hint: What did Turing say the teacher wouldn't understand?
evidence: Hand-coded rules vs educated child machine

scenarios.title: Score the Storage Bet
scenarios.situation: Turing predicted machines with about 1GB of storage by 2000.
choices: Storage doesn't matter for AI.
Terribly — nowhere close.

Roughly right: by 2000, 1GB was ordinary (hard drives, RAM growth) — remarkably close for a 1950 forecast. The METHOD of prediction (extrapolating storage growth) worked even where the test bar proved gameable.
He meant 1GB of RAM specifically.
scenarios.why: The correct approach scores fairly: the capacity forecast was impressively close — consumer machines around 2000 commonly had ~1GB-scale storage. Separate this win from the shakier 30%-fooling prediction.
scenarios.hint: What did he get right vs what proved gameable?

scenarios.title: The Pop Version
scenarios.situation: A headline: 'AI passes the Turing test!' The 'test': one journalist chatted 3 minutes with no human control and was impressed.
choices: Turing's test had controls for a reason: timed interaction, human baseline, statistical misidentification rates. A 3-minute impressed-journalist demo satisfies none of them — it's marketing wearing a lab coat.
The test is outdated anyway.
Journalists can't judge AI.
Celebrate — the test is passed.
scenarios.why: The correct approach checks the controls before the conclusion: no baseline, no fixed protocol, no statistics = no test. Turing's contribution was the experimental frame, and headlines keep discarding it.
scenarios.hint: Which of Turing's controls are present here?
evidence: 'Passes the Turing test' — 3 min, no controls

scenarios.title: Would Turing Call It Intelligent?
scenarios.situation: You're asked whether Turing would call a modern LLM 'intelligent.'
choices: No — he'd see through the trick.

Turing would ask about the CONTROLS: under his specified conditions (5-min, human baseline, 30% rate), then note his test was always a sufficient-condition probe, not a definition of intelligence — and that his deeper bet was on learning machines, which LLMs vindicate in paradigm if not in detail.
He'd refuse to answer.
Yes — it passes his test, case closed.
scenarios.why: The correct approach avoids both anachronism and dismissal: apply his controls honestly, remember the test probes behavior not essence, and credit the paradigm win (learning machines) while noting the bar's gameability.
scenarios.hint: Was the test a definition or a probe?
objectives: Treat test as probe not definition

domains.description: Turing's 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence': the imitation game, learning machines, objections, and honest scoring.

domains.name: Enigma and Bletchley Park

scenarios.title: The Reflector's Gift
scenarios.situation: Enigma's reflector meant no letter could encrypt to itself. German designers saw this as a feature.
scenarios.prompt: How did Bletchley turn it into a weapon?
choices: They couldn't — it was purely a German advantage.
It halved the keyspace directly.
Crib placement: slide guessed plaintext along the cipher — any alignment where a letter matches itself is IMPOSSIBLE, so most positions are eliminated instantly. The 'feature' became a sieve.
It made the machine slower.
scenarios.why: The correct approach exploits the constraint: no-self-encryption turns crib-dragging into rapid elimination. A design choice meant to simplify operation handed attackers a powerful filter — constraints cut both ways.
scenarios.hint: How do you use an impossibility as a filter?
evidence: Reflector: L never encrypts to L

scenarios.title: Could They Brute-Force It?
scenarios.situation: Enigma's keyspace was ~10^23. A 1940s team considers brute force.
choices: At even a million keys/second (fantasy for 1940), 10^23 keys takes ~3 billion years. Brute force was never an option — Bletchley won via cribs, procedural flaws, and constraint-guided search, not enumeration.
Feasible on weekends.
The Poles already did it by hand.
Feasible — just build more Bombes.
scenarios.why: The correct approach does the arithmetic: 10^23 / 10^6 / 3.15e7 ≈ 3e9 years. The lesson generalizes — keyspace size is why cryptography works; Bletchley's genius was never trying the front door.
scenarios.hint: Do the division: 10^23 keys at 10^6 per second?

scenarios.title: From Crib to Menu
scenarios.situation: You have a crib: WETTER aligns with cipher ETJRR at some position.
scenarios.prompt: How does this become a Bombe 'menu'?
choices: Feed the whole message into the Bombe.

The crib's letter pairings (W->E, E->T, T->J...) form chains through the plugboard — linked into LOOPS. The menu encodes these loops; the Bombe tests rotor positions for loop consistency, discarding inconsistent ones.
Guess the plugboard directly.
Menus are just the crib written out.
scenarios.why: The correct approach builds the constraint network: each crib pairing implies plugboard relations, and loops make those relations testable — a position is viable only if every loop closes consistently. The menu is the loop diagram, wired.
scenarios.hint: What makes a rotor position testable rather than guessable?

scenarios.title: Placing the Crib
scenarios.situation: Cipher: XQJZMP. Suspected plaintext: WETTER.
choices: Cribs can't be placed — they're guesses.
Position 1 — always start at the beginning.
Anywhere — cribs slide freely.

Only positions where NO letter matches itself: X-W,Q-E,J-T,Z-T,M-E,P-R — all differ, so position 1 is possible; any alignment with a self-match is impossible. The reflector rule prunes placements before the Bombe runs.
scenarios.why: The correct approach applies the no-self-encryption filter to each candidate alignment: it's a cheap pre-test eliminating most positions. Cribs were often stereotyped message openings (weather reports) — predictable plaintext, the operator's other gift.
scenarios.hint: Which alignments does the reflector rule kill?

scenarios.title: The Human Factor
scenarios.situation: Historians argue Hut 8's biggest breaks came from operator errors, not machine attacks. A student finds this disappointing.
choices: The operators were the system: Enigma's math was sound, so the attack surface WAS procedure — cillies, doubled keys, stereotyped messages. Targeting the weakest link is the essence of applied cryptanalysis, not a consolation prize.
Turing would have preferred pure math.
The math was actually broken too.
It IS disappointing — real cryptanalysis should be pure math.
scenarios.why: The correct approach internalizes the security lesson: systems break at their weakest link, and the weakest link is usually human. Bletchley's triumph was operational thinking — attacking the system as deployed, not as designed.
scenarios.hint: Where does a sound cipher actually break?

scenarios.title: Measuring Hut 8
scenarios.situation: Claims about Hut 8 range from 'won the war' to 'marginal.'
scenarios.prompt: What's the honest assessment of the naval Enigma work?
choices: It single-handedly won the war.
It was marginal — convoys would've survived anyway.

Significant and measurable: naval Enigma intelligence (Ultra) demonstrably rerouted convoys around U-boat packs, with historians crediting it for shortening the Atlantic campaign — decisive contribution within a vast Allied effort, not solo victory.
Impossible to assess.
scenarios.why: The correct approach avoids both hagiography and dismissal: Ultra's convoy-rerouting is documented and quantified by historians, while 'won the war alone' ignores everything else. Honest impact assessment holds both.
scenarios.hint: What's documented vs what's mythology?

scenarios.title: The Polish Priority
scenarios.situation: A popular account credits Turing with breaking Enigma first in 1939.
scenarios.prompt: Who actually broke it first, and why does it matter?
choices: Turing, in 1939.

The Poles — Rejewski, Różycki, Zygalski — broke Enigma in 1932 with the bomba and Zygalski sheets, and shared everything with Britain/France in July 1939. Turing built on their foundation; honest history starts in Warsaw, not Bletchley.
The French, alone.
Nobody before Bletchley.
scenarios.why: The correct approach gives Warsaw its due: Rejewski's permutation theory cracked Enigma seven years before Turing's arrival, and the July 1939 handover (including a rebuilt Enigma) jump-started Bletchley. Turing's genius operated on Polish foundations.
scenarios.hint: What did Britain receive in July 1939?
evidence: Polish Biuro Szyfrów broke Enigma 1932; shared July 1939

domains.description: The machine, the procedures, the Bombe, and honest historiography of Turing's wartime work.

domains.name: Cryptography After Turing

scenarios.title: When to Use the One-Time Pad
scenarios.situation: A client wants 'unbreakable encryption' for their 10,000 daily customer transactions and proposes OTP.
choices: Great choice — deploy OTP everywhere.

OTP is wrong here: perfect secrecy demands a truly random key as long as each message, never reused — distributing 10,000 fresh keys daily IS the secure-channel problem all over again. Use AES for bulk data; reserve OTP for tiny, ultra-high-value traffic.
OTP is broken — use ROT13.
Use OTP but reuse keys to save effort.
scenarios.why: The correct approach names the real cost: OTP doesn't eliminate key distribution, it relocates it. For bulk traffic, modern ciphers give practical security without the impossible logistics.
scenarios.hint: What problem does OTP solve vs relocate?

scenarios.title: The Fundamental Problem
scenarios.situation: Why is key distribution called the fundamental problem of pre-1976 cryptography?
scenarios.prompt: What was circular about the old world?
choices: Nobody thought about it.
Keys were too short.
Math was too weak.

Secure communication needed a shared secret, but sharing the secret needed a secure channel — the circular dependency. Every system (codebooks, couriers, Enigma's daily keys) was a workaround; public key broke the circle.
scenarios.why: The correct approach states the circularity: to communicate securely you need a shared secret, to share the secret you need secure communication. Codebooks and couriers managed the circle; Diffie-Hellman dissolved it.
scenarios.hint: What was circular about the old world?

scenarios.title: What Was Delilah?
scenarios.situation: A student confuses Delilah with the Bombe. Set it straight.
scenarios.prompt: How do you set it straight?
choices: They're the same machine.
Delilah was an early computer.

Delilah was Turing's postwar portable secure-VOICE system — speech encryption for field use, built after Bletchley. The Bombe attacked Enigma keys; Delilah protected voice. Different wars' problems, different engineering.
Delilah was a cipher like Enigma.
scenarios.why: The correct approach separates the artifacts by purpose and era: Bombe (1940, attack Enigma), Delilah (postwar, protect voice). Conflating them erases Turing's engineering breadth.
scenarios.hint: Attack vs protect — which was which?

scenarios.title: The Secret Algorithm
scenarios.situation: A vendor pitches: 'Our proprietary cipher is secure because nobody knows how it works.'
choices: Kerckhoffs's principle: security must reside in the KEY, not algorithm secrecy. Secret algorithms can't be peer-reviewed, hide flaws, and leak anyway (reverse engineering, insiders). Demand open, analyzed crypto with secret keys.
Ask for a discount.
Proprietary is always better.
Buy it — secrecy is security.
scenarios.why: The correct approach invokes Kerckhoffs: every secret algorithm in history leaked or harbored flaws; open algorithms survive adversarial review. 'Nobody knows how it works' includes your defenders.
scenarios.hint: Who else doesn't know how it works — including whom?

scenarios.title: What Public Key Solved
scenarios.situation: Before public-key crypto, two strangers wanting secure email faced what problem — and what changed?
scenarios.prompt: What problem did they face, and what changed?
choices: No problem — they just called each other.

They needed a pre-shared secret with no secure way to agree on one at a distance — the key-distribution circle. Public key (DH/RSA) lets strangers establish secrets over public channels: publish public keys, keep private keys secret.
Email didn't exist.
They used weaker ciphers happily.
scenarios.why: The correct approach centers the stranger problem: the internet is strangers communicating. Without public key, every pair needs a prior secure meeting — unscalable. With it, the web's security model works.
scenarios.hint: Why is 'strangers' the key word?
evidence: Two strangers, secure email, no prior contact

scenarios.title: The 'Unbreakable' Vendor
scenarios.situation: A vendor claims their new cipher is 'unbreakable, military-grade, proprietary.'
choices: All ciphers are unbreakable now.
Only the military can judge.
Accept — military-grade is convincing.

Enigma was called unbreakable too — by its makers, with real math behind it. It fell to procedures, cribs, and statistics, not broken math. Demand: open design, peer review, and threat modeling of the DEPLOYED system, not adjectives.
scenarios.why: The correct approach runs Enigma's lesson: 'unbreakable' described the math, and the math wasn't the attack surface. Evaluate the deployed system — procedures, keys, side channels — not the adjectives.
scenarios.hint: What did 'unbreakable' mean for Enigma, and where did it break?

scenarios.title: Banburismus Today
scenarios.situation: Where does Turing's statistical scoring method (accumulate weak evidence into strong verdicts) live on today?
scenarios.prompt: Where does the method live on today?
choices: Nowhere — statistics moved on.
Only in history books.

Everywhere: spam filters (Bayesian scoring), intrusion detection (anomaly accumulation), side-channel attacks (trace averaging) — Banburismus's 'weak evidence added up' is the standard playbook of applied statistics in security.
Only in cryptography.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes the pattern, not the artifact: sequential Bayesian updating underlies half of applied security. Turing did it with punched sheets; we do it with GPUs — same mathematics.
scenarios.hint: What's the abstract pattern, stripped of 1940?

domains.description: From wartime ciphers to modern crypto: one-time pads, Delilah, public key, and Turing's statistical legacy.

domains.name: The Turing Test

scenarios.title: Design a Fair Test
scenarios.situation: You're commissioned to run a rigorous modern imitation game with real stakes.
choices: The smartest AI available.
Celebrity judges.
A chatbot, a judge, and a press release.

Text-only channel, human baseline (judges try to spot the human too), fixed interaction time, pre-registered misidentification-rate statistic, blinded judges — without each, results are anecdote, not evidence.
scenarios.why: The correct approach rebuilds Turing's controls for the modern era: the human baseline calibrates judge fallibility, fixed time bounds the interaction, and pre-registered statistics prevent moving goalposts. Controls are what separate science from demo.
scenarios.hint: Which element, if missing, makes it marketing?
evidence: Rigorous modern imitation game, real stakes

scenarios.title: Does the Room Refute the Test?
scenarios.situation: Searle's Chinese room: perfect symbol manipulation, zero understanding. Does it refute the Turing test?
choices: Yes — definitively. AI is dead.

It targets the test's PHILOSOPHICAL interpretation (behavior = understanding), not its methodological value: the test still measures behavioral indistinguishability, which is useful regardless. The systems reply further blurs Searle's conclusion — the debate continues.
No — Searle was confused.
The room proves machines understand.
scenarios.why: The correct approach separates levels: Searle attacks 'passing implies understanding,' which the test never strictly claimed — Turing offered behavior as a sufficient probe, not a metaphysical certificate. Both can be right at different levels.
scenarios.hint: What exactly does the room argue against?

scenarios.title: The Model 'Passes'
scenarios.situation: A modern LLM hits 45% misidentification in a well-controlled 5-minute test. Headlines declare machine intelligence achieved.
choices: A controlled pass is genuinely informative: it shows behavioral indistinguishability under those conditions — a real milestone. But it doesn't settle understanding or consciousness, and the conditions (5 min, text-only) bound the claim. Report the result, bound the interpretation.
The test was flawed, ignore it.
Longer tests would fail, so it means nothing.
Machine intelligence is achieved — headlines are right.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats a controlled pass as data, not coronation: the achievement is real within its bounds, and the bounds are everything. Turing's frame invites exactly this — empirical results, carefully interpreted.
scenarios.hint: What was actually demonstrated, precisely?

scenarios.title: The Lovelace Test
scenarios.situation: A proposed alternative: the Lovelace test — an AI passes only if it creates something its programmers can't explain. Fairer than Turing's?
choices: Lovelace was wrong about everything.
Yes — much better, adopt it.

It's a different probe, not a replacement: Lovelace tests ORIGINATION/surprise, Turing tests BEHAVIORAL indistinguishability. They measure different things; 'fairer' depends on what you want to know. Note modern models already surprise their makers routinely.
No — creativity is untestable.
scenarios.why: The correct approach compares what each test operationalizes: surprise vs indistinguishability are different questions. And the surprise criterion is already partially met — which tells you something about the criterion's sharpness.
scenarios.hint: What does each test actually measure?

scenarios.title: Building the Deceiver
scenarios.situation: Your team could build a system optimized specifically to fool elderly users into thinking it's their grandchild. It would 'pass' easily.
choices: It's fine if it helps them feel less lonely.
Only illegal if caught.
Great product — ship it.

Passing isn't the problem — deception of vulnerable people is: the ethical issue is the TARGET and PURPOSE, not the capability. Turing's test as science needs consenting judges; as a product, fooling the vulnerable is fraud-adjacent regardless of test scores.
scenarios.why: The correct approach separates capability from deployment ethics: the same indistinguishability that's scientifically interesting becomes harmful aimed at the vulnerable without consent. Tests need willing participants; products need honest framing.
scenarios.hint: Who is being fooled, and did they consent?

scenarios.title: What the Test Can't See
scenarios.situation: A system passes every behavioral test but its creators confirm it has no persistent goals, no self-model, no inner experience. Problem for the test?
scenarios.prompt: Is this a problem for the test?
choices: No — passing is all that matters.

It reveals the test's boundary: behavioral indistinguishability underdetermines inner life — the test was designed to sidestep consciousness, not detect it. Passing tells you about performance, nothing about experience. That's a feature of the design, honestly stated.
The creators are lying.
Inner experience doesn't exist.
scenarios.why: The correct approach states the boundary plainly: Turing deliberately excluded the inner from the testable. A test that sidesteps consciousness can't discover it — use the test for what it measures, not what it brackets.
scenarios.hint: What did Turing deliberately exclude?
evidence: Passes behaviorally; no inner life (per creators)

scenarios.title: Why Operationalize?
scenarios.situation: A philosopher insists: 'Before testing machine intelligence, define intelligence properly.'
choices: Proper definitions of contested concepts rarely precede inquiry — they FOLLOW it. Turing's move: replace the unanswerable with the testable, learn from results, refine concepts empirically. Waiting for perfect definitions is how fields stall for centuries.
Philosophy is useless.
Intelligence is indefinable.
He'd agree — definitions first.
scenarios.why: The correct approach defends operationalism: science routinely starts with rough operational handles and sharpens them through experiment. The demand for prior perfect definition is a stalling tactic, however sincerely meant.
scenarios.hint: Do definitions precede or follow inquiry?

domains.description: The imitation game done right: the specified test, what it proves, Searle's challenge, and modern evaluation.

domains.name: Wartime Computing

scenarios.title: What Colossus Was
scenarios.situation: A museum plaque calls Colossus 'the world's first programmable computer, built by Alan Turing.'
choices: Three: (1) not general-purpose/programmable in the modern sense — special-purpose Tunny-breaker; (2) built by Tommy Flowers, not Turing; (3) 'first computer' needs heavy qualification. Honest plaque: first large-scale electronic digital computer, Flowers, for Tunny.
One — Turing didn't build it.
Two — it wasn't electronic.
None — accurate plaque.
scenarios.why: The correct approach counts precisely: purpose (special, not general), builder (Flowers, not Turing), and 'first' (electronic digital at scale — qualified). Each error distorts a different lesson.
scenarios.hint: Check builder, purpose, and 'first' separately.

scenarios.title: Why Tunny Needed Machines
scenarios.situation: Tunny's keyspace and traffic volume made hand methods hopeless. What specifically forced mechanization?
choices: Machines are always better.
The Germans used more operators.
Hand methods were banned.

Scale: Tutte's statistical attack required counting coincidences across thousands of characters at many wheel positions — combinatorial drudgery no human team could sustain at operational tempo. Electronics didn't add cleverness; they added SPEED to proven statistics.
scenarios.why: The correct approach names scale as the driver: the method existed (Testery, by hand), but operational tempo demanded electronic speed. Colossus mechanized proven statistics — automate the proven, not the hoped.
scenarios.hint: What did the Testery prove before Colossus existed?

scenarios.title: Turing's Actual Role
scenarios.situation: Where did Turing actually sit in the Tunny/Colossus effort?
choices: He led Newmanry day-to-day.

Consultant with key breakthroughs: Turing contributed ideas (including 'Turingery,' a wheel-setting method) and advised, while Newman ran the section, Tutte did the statistics, and Flowers built the machine. Influence without ownership — the honest credit.
He had no involvement.
He built Colossus himself.
scenarios.why: The correct approach places him precisely: consulting genius, not project lead. Inflating his role erases Newman, Tutte, and Flowers; minimizing it erases real contributions. Precision IS the tribute.
scenarios.hint: Who ran it, who built it, who consulted?
evidence: Newman ran, Tutte analyzed, Flowers built, Turing consulted

scenarios.title: Flowers vs the Experts
scenarios.situation: Experts told Tommy Flowers that 1,500+ valves could never work reliably. He built Colossus anyway.
choices: Experts are always wrong.
Flowers got lucky.

Informed engineering judgment can beat consensus: Flowers KNEW valves from telephone-exchange experience (they're reliable if never switched off thermally) — domain expertise over generic skepticism. Bet on tested knowledge, not on contrarianism for its own sake.
Reliability doesn't matter.
scenarios.why: The correct approach distinguishes informed dissent from crank contrarianism: Flowers had specific, tested reasons (Post Office valve experience). The lesson is 'trust deep domain evidence over committee opinion,' not 'ignore experts.'
scenarios.hint: What did Flowers know that the experts didn't?

scenarios.title: Tutte's Feat
scenarios.situation: Bill Tutte, age 24, reconstructed the Lorenz machine's complete logical structure having never seen one — from a single depth. Assess this.
scenarios.prompt: How do you assess this feat?
choices: Routine — any analyst could do it.

The deepest single cryptanalytic inference of the war: from 4000 characters of key-reuse, Tutte deduced 12 wheels, their grouping, and stepping — pure structural reverse-engineering. It made Colossus possible; without it, no machine to build.
He had a captured machine.
Turing did it for him.
scenarios.why: The correct approach grasps the magnitude: inferring an unseen machine's full logic from one operator error is among the finest analytical feats on record. Colossus was built to automate TUTTE's statistics — the method preceded the machine.
scenarios.hint: What did he have to work with?

scenarios.title: The Cost of Secrecy
scenarios.situation: Was the decades-long classification of Colossus 'worth it'?
choices: Both true: wartime secrecy was arguably necessary; the DECADES-long continuation cost Flowers recognition and funding, distorted computing's origin story, and left pioneers unrewarded. Necessity doesn't erase cost — honest accounting holds both.
Historians exaggerate the cost.
Obviously yes — security first.
Obviously no — openness always wins.
scenarios.why: The correct approach refuses the binary: classify the wartime need separately from the peacetime continuation. The bill — careers, narratives, momentum — was real even if the original decision was justified.
scenarios.hint: Separate wartime need from peacetime continuation.

scenarios.title: Wartime to ACE
scenarios.situation: Which wartime lesson MOST shaped Turing's 1945 ACE design?
choices: Enigma rotors directly.
Camouflage techniques.
Radio procedures.

That electronics at scale WORK (Flowers proved valves reliable) and that programs belong in memory (his own 1936 UTM) — ACE fused Bletchley's engineering proof with his theoretical architecture. The war didn't just delay computing; it de-risked it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach connects the dots: ACE's stored program = UTM made real; its electronic ambition = Flowers's proof of valve reliability. The design was theory validated by wartime engineering — neither alone sufficed.
scenarios.hint: Which ACE feature came from theory, which from the war?

domains.name: Turing's Modern Legacy

scenarios.title: ACE's Core Innovation
scenarios.situation: What was the most architecturally distinctive idea in Turing's 1945 ACE design?
choices: It was the first transistor computer.
Bigger valves than Colossus.
Minimal hardware with maximal software: a terse instruction set, subroutines as first-class, programs fully in memory — pushing complexity into code for speed. The 1936 universal machine, engineered.
It used punch cards exclusively.
scenarios.why: The correct approach sees ACE as the UTM built: stored program as architecture, subroutines as structure, simplicity as speed. The philosophy — hardware minimal, software maximal — prefigures RISC by decades.
scenarios.hint: Where had Turing described this architecture before?

scenarios.title: Spots from Nowhere
scenarios.situation: How does reaction-diffusion produce leopard spots from uniform chemistry?
choices: Local activation + lateral inhibition: an activator that spreads slowly amplifies itself nearby, while a fast-diffusing inhibitor suppresses it at distance — uniform soup breaks into spots spontaneously. Pattern without a blueprint.
Spots are random mutations.
Chemistry can't make patterns.
The leopard's DNA paints each spot individually.
scenarios.why: The correct approach grasps symmetry-breaking: uniform + noise + local-rules = pattern. No painter, no plan — the spots self-organize. Turing showed order doesn't need an orderer.
scenarios.hint: Where's the 'design' in the design?

scenarios.title: Why His Name?
scenarios.situation: Why is computing's highest prize named for Turing rather than, say, von Neumann?
choices: Turing had better publicity.
Von Neumann declined the honor.
It's arbitrary — any founder would do.

Because the field's foundations are Turing's: the definition of computation, the universal machine, undecidability, AI's framing. Von Neumann built crucially ON those foundations. The award names the root, not a branch.
scenarios.why: The correct approach answers foundationally: computability theory, the UTM, and AI's operational framing are the soil everything grows in. Naming honors origins — and the field chose correctly.
scenarios.hint: What grows from his work that doesn't grow from others'?

scenarios.title: Teaching the Injustice
scenarios.situation: How should a technical course teach Turing's 1952 prosecution?
choices: Dwell on it exclusively — the math is secondary.

Plainly and fully, proportionate: state the facts (prosecution, chemical castration, clearance revoked, death at 41), the reckoning timeline (2009/2013/2017), and the cost — then return to the ideas. The injustice is part of the story, not a detour from it.
Present it as ancient history with no lessons.
Skip it — keep the course technical.
scenarios.why: The correct approach integrates rather than isolates: the prosecution explains lost years and lost work, and the pardon timeline shows institutional reckoning. Facts stated plainly carry their own weight — no editorializing needed.
scenarios.hint: What does the timeline itself teach?

scenarios.title: Which Field Owes Most?
scenarios.situation: Four claimants: AI, cryptography, computability theory, mathematical biology. Which owes Turing most?
scenarios.prompt: Which owes most — or is the question wrong?
choices: The question is malformed: each field's debt is foundational but different — computability IS his definitions, crypto got his methods, AI got his framing, biology got a founding paper. 'Most' depends on the metric; the remarkable fact is one person founded pieces of all four.
Biology — morphogenesis rules.
Cryptography — the war was biggest.
AI — obviously.
scenarios.why: The correct approach rejects the ranking game: foundational debts don't sum to a winner. The insight is the BREADTH — four fields, one mind, each debt structural. That's the actual marvel.
scenarios.hint: What would 'most' even mean here?

scenarios.title: Verify the Quote
scenarios.situation: 'We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done.' — widely attributed to Turing. Use it?
choices: Yes — it's inspiring and famous.
No — it's misattributed.

It's genuine — the closing lines of 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950), verifiable in the text. USE it, and cite the paper: the one famous Turing quote that's real. (Most others circulating are fake — always verify.)
Quotes don't matter.
scenarios.why: The correct approach verifies: this one is real (1950 paper's ending), which is precisely why it's worth using — and the verification habit matters because most circulating 'Turing quotes' are invented.
scenarios.hint: How do you check a quote's provenance?
evidence: 'We can only see a short distance ahead...'

scenarios.title: The £50 Note
scenarios.situation: In 2021 Turing joined the Bank of England's £50 note. What does that signify — beyond honor?
choices: He's the first scientist on currency.
It's just PR for the bank.
Nothing — currency faces are random.

A civilization's honor roll: currency faces signal who a society credits for its modernity. Turing on the £50 — alongside the Bombe, the UTM, formulae — says Britain now traces its digital age to him. Note the arc: 1952 prosecution to 2021 celebration.
scenarios.why: The correct approach reads the symbolism: the note's imagery (Bombe, formulae, the 1950 quote) compresses his whole arc into a pocket monument — and the 1952-to-2021 contrast is the story of a society revising its judgment.
scenarios.hint: What changed between 1952 and 2021?

lessons.title: Alan Turing — Core concepts
concepts: The Turing machine (1936) is an abstract model of computation — an infinite tape, a head, and a state table — not a physical device. Its power comes from the universal machine: one fixed design that can simulate any other machine, which is the theoretical basis of the stored-program computer.

Computability has hard limits. The halting problem — deciding whether an arbitrary program terminates — is undecidable: Turing proved no general algorithm can solve it, using a diagonal argument in which a program is built to contradict any claimed decider.

At Bletchley Park, Turing turned theory into machines: the Bombe (with Gordon Welchman) mechanized the search over Enigma rotor settings, exploiting the reflector's no-self-encryption property and guessed plaintext ('cribs') to rule out impossible positions.

The Turing test (1950, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence') proposes a behavioral, comparative criterion for machine intelligence: a blinded interrogator tries to distinguish machine from human by text conversation. It tests imitation under controlled conditions, not consciousness.

Morphogenesis (1952): Turing's reaction-diffusion model shows how local chemical interactions plus diffusion can spontaneously generate biological patterns — an early mathematical treatment of emergence, far outside computing.

Turing's through-line is the formalization of process: what can be computed, what can be decided, what can be broken, what can be imitated, what can self-organize. Each result draws a boundary — and boundaries are where engineering lives.

example.code:
python3 - <<'EOF'
# A tiny Turing machine: binary incrementer
tape = list('1011') + ['_']; head = len(tape)-2
state = 'carry'
while state == 'carry':
    if tape[head] == '1': tape[head]='0'; head -= 1
    elif tape[head] == '0': tape[head]='1'; state='done'
    else: tape[head]='1'; state='done'
print(''.join(tape).rstrip('_'))  # 1100
EOF
example.walkthrough: This is a literal Turing machine: a tape, a head, and a state table ('carry'). It adds one to a binary number by the same scan-and-flip procedure the abstract model describes — the model is executable, not just philosophical.

pitfalls: Common trap: calling the Turing machine a physical invention — it is a mathematical definition of computability from 1936, predating electronic computers.
Common trap: treating the Turing test as a test of consciousness or understanding — Turing proposed an imitation game, a behavioral comparison, nothing more.
Common trap: crediting Turing alone with breaking Enigma — it was a large team effort building on Polish cryptanalysts (notably Marian Rejewski), and the Bombe industrialized an existing attack.
Common trap: reading 'undecidable' as 'hard' — the halting problem is not merely difficult, it is provably impossible for a general decider; tools that work do so on restricted inputs.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Alan Turing move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence

lessons.title: 1936: 'On Computable Numbers'
concepts: Turing wrote the paper to settle the Entscheidungsproblem — whether a definite method could decide all mathematical statements
His strategy: define 'method' precisely with an imaginary machine, then prove the limits of what any such machine can do
The paper introduced both the Turing machine and the universal machine — the stored-program concept — in one stroke
Context: Alonzo Church reached similar results via lambda calculus the same year; the equivalence of their models became the Church-Turing thesis

example.code:
Paper roadmap:
  1. Define the machine (sections 1-2)
  2. Show it computes the computable numbers
  3. Build the universal machine (section 6)
  4. Prove the decision problem unsolvable (section 8)
Read it in this order — it's more readable than its reputation.
example.walkthrough: Don't mythologize: Turing built on Gödel, Church, and Hilbert's questions — genius inside a conversation, not from nowhere.

pitfalls: Treating the machine as a blueprint — it was a definition for proofs, not an engineering proposal
Skipping the Entscheidungsproblem context — the paper answers a specific question
Confusing 1936 with 1950 — the machine paper and the AI paper are 14 years apart
lessons.try_it: Write one paragraph: what specific question was Turing answering in 1936?

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Turing Machine
concepts: Four parts: an infinite tape divided into cells, a read/write head, a state register, and a finite transition table
A transition rule: (current state, symbol read) -> (write symbol, move L/R, next state) — the entire 'program'
The machine is deterministic: each (state, symbol) pair has exactly one rule — no choices, no randomness in the basic model
Formally a 7-tuple, but think operationally: it's a rule-follower with unbounded memory and finite control

example.code:
Rule format:
  (q0, 1) -> (0, R, q1)
  'in state q0 reading 1: write 0,
   move right, enter q1'
Every program is a set of such rules.
example.walkthrough: The infinite tape isn't a claim about hardware — it's the idealization that memory is never the fundamental limit.

pitfalls: Adding 'intelligence' to the model — it's deliberately mindless; that's the point
Confusing states with tape symbols — states are the control, symbols are the data
Thinking infinite tape means infinite speed — steps are still one at a time
lessons.try_it: Write the transition rules for a machine that erases its entire tape and halts.

lessons.title: Worked Example: The Binary Incrementer
concepts: Task: given binary on the tape, add one. States: q0 (scan right to the end), q1 (carry leftward), qH (halt)
Trace 1011: scan right past all digits, step left, flip trailing 1s to 0, flip first 0 (or blank) to 1, halt -> 1100
The trace IS the computation: following rules mechanically produces the answer — this is what 'algorithm' means formally

example.code:
Trace 1011 -> 1100:
  q0: 1,0,1,1 then blank -> q1, move L
  q1 on 1 -> write 0, move L (twice)
  q1 on 0 -> write 1, HALT
  tape: 1 1 0 0. Done.
example.walkthrough: Trace by hand before trusting intuition — hand-tracing is how you debug state machines forever.

pitfalls: Losing track of head position — mark it every step
Forgetting the blank-to-1 rule — incrementing 111 needs the extra digit
Skipping the trace — reading rules feels like understanding; tracing proves it
lessons.try_it: Trace the incrementer on 111 by hand. Verify you get 1000.

lessons.title: The Universal Machine: Software Is Born
concepts: A universal Turing machine (UTM) reads another machine's description from its tape and simulates it — one machine runs all programs
This is the stored-program concept: program and data share the same tape/memory — the founding idea of modern computers
Consequence: an interpreter is a UTM; your Python runtime simulates Python programs exactly as a UTM simulates machines
Turing proved universality constructively — he gave the simulation method, not just an existence claim

example.code:
UTM sketch:
  tape: [machine description][input data]
  UTM loop: read current simulated state+symbol,
  look up the rule in the description,
  apply it to the simulated tape
Simulation, all the way down.
example.walkthrough: Every layer of modern computing (emulators, VMs, interpreters) is this 1936 idea in engineering clothes.

pitfalls: 'Universal' meaning all-powerful — it means all-computations, still bound by computability limits
Thinking von Neumann invented stored program alone — Turing's UTM is the theoretical ancestor
Confusing universality with efficiency — simulation can be exponentially slower
lessons.try_it: Name three universal machines you use daily (hint: interpreter, VM, browser).

lessons.title: What Turing Machines Can't Do (Preview)
concepts: The model defines the boundary of computation itself: anything uncomputable here is uncomputable by any physical means (per the thesis)
Famous limit: the halting problem — no machine decides whether arbitrary machines halt — proved by Turing in the same paper
The diagonal argument is the proof technique: assume a decider exists, build a machine that contradicts it
This isn't a flaw in the model — it's a discovery about reality: some questions have no algorithmic answer, period

example.code:
Halting proof sketch:
  assume H decides halts(P, input)
  build D: if H(D,D) says halts, loop forever;
         else halt
  D halts iff D doesn't halt — contradiction
  so H cannot exist.
example.walkthrough: Learn to love impossibility results: they tell you where not to waste your life.

pitfalls: Reading 'uncomputable' as 'hard' — it means impossible in principle, not difficult
Thinking faster hardware helps — no speed solves the halting problem
Skipping ahead without the model — the proof needs the machine definition first
lessons.try_it: Explain in two sentences why no perfect virus detector can exist.

lessons.title: Decidable vs Recognizable
concepts: Decidable: a machine that always halts with yes/no — total certainty, always
Recognizable (semi-decidable): halts with 'yes' on yes-instances, may loop forever on no-instances — half an answer
Every decidable language is recognizable; the converse fails — the halting language is the canonical counterexample
Intuition: deciding means ruling out; recognizing means confirming — ruling out is strictly harder

example.code:
Classify:
  'does P halt on x?' -> recognizable (simulate; yes if it halts)
  ...but NOT decidable (Turing, 1936)
  'is x even?' -> decidable (always halts)
Ask: does my decider always halt?
example.walkthrough: When someone claims a decider, ask the killer question: 'does it halt on every input?'

pitfalls: Conflating 'we can check yes' with 'we can decide' — the gap is the whole subject
Thinking recognizable = useless — many real tools are recognizers (they find bugs but can't prove absence)
Forgetting the complement: decidable languages are closed under complement; recognizable ones aren't
lessons.try_it: Classify: 'this program prints hello' — decidable, recognizable, or neither? Why?

lessons.title: The Halting Problem
concepts: Statement: no Turing machine decides, for all (P, x), whether P halts on x
Proof: assume H exists; build D that halts iff H says D doesn't halt on itself — contradiction, so H can't exist
This is diagonalization in action: D is constructed to differ from every machine H claims to judge
Turing proved it in 1936 — before any physical computer existed; it's about computation itself, not technology

example.code:
The proof, tightly:
  1. Suppose H(P,x) decides halting
  2. D(x): if H(x,x) halts -> loop; else halt
  3. D(D): halts iff H says not iff D loops
  4. Contradiction -> no such H
example.walkthrough: Memorize the proof's SHAPE (assume, diagonalize, contradict) — it recurs across undecidability.

pitfalls: 'We just haven't found H yet' — the proof shows it can't exist, not that it's hard
Thinking it limits only Turing machines — it limits all computation per the thesis
Confusing halting with 'slow' — it's about never, not late
lessons.try_it: Write the 4-line proof from memory. Check against the lesson.

lessons.title: Diagonalization: Cantor's Weapon
concepts: Cantor (1891): the reals are uncountable — list them, build a real differing from each listed one at position n
Turing's move: the same diagonal trick, but machines instead of reals — D differs from every machine H adjudicates
