The pattern: assume enumeration/decision exists -> construct the diagonal object -> contradiction
Diagonalization proves uncountability AND undecidability — one technique, two revolutions

example.code:
Cantor's diagonal:
  r1 = 0.1415...
  r2 = 0.2653...
  r3 = 0.1618...
  d  = 0.274... (differ at digit n from rn)
  d is real, d not in the list.
example.walkthrough: When you see 'assume we can list/decide all X,' reach for the diagonal — it's the standard weapon.

pitfalls: Thinking diagonalization is about geometry — it's about self-reference defeating enumeration
Applying it where enumerations don't exist — the setup matters
Missing that D must be constructible — the diagonal object has to be a valid machine
lessons.try_it: Prove the power set of naturals is uncountable via diagonalization.

lessons.title: Reductions: Proving Hardness by Translation
concepts: Reduction: to prove L undecidable, show that deciding L would let you decide a known-undecidable problem (usually HALT)
Direction matters: reduce FROM the known-hard problem TO your problem — 'HALT <= L' means L is at least as hard as HALT
Template: assume decider for L; build a machine that uses it to decide HALT; contradiction; L undecidable
Reductions also order difficulty among decidable problems — the same idea powers NP-completeness

example.code:
Prove 'does P ever print 42?' undecidable:
  assume decider A for PRINTS-42
  to decide HALT(P,x): build Q that runs P(x),
    then prints 42; A(Q) decides HALT
  contradiction -> PRINTS-42 undecidable
example.walkthrough: Master the template sentence: 'If I could decide L, I could decide HALT by...'

pitfalls: Reducing the wrong direction — decide-HALT-using-L proves L hard, not the reverse
Forgetting the construction must be computable — the translator is itself a program
Hand-waving the contradiction — spell out what breaks
lessons.try_it: Prove 'does P halt on all inputs?' undecidable via reduction from HALT.

lessons.title: What Undecidability Means for Practice
concepts: Rice's theorem: ANY nontrivial semantic property of programs is undecidable — behavior questions have no perfect deciders
Real tools (linters, analyzers) are recognizers/heuristics: they catch some bugs, miss others, sometimes false-alarm — necessarily
The practical move: restrict the domain — decidable fragments (finite-state, type systems) trade expressiveness for guarantees
Undecidability is a map of where not to dig: don't build products promising perfect detection of behavioral properties

example.code:
Rice's hit list (all undecidable):
  virus detection, equivalence checking,
  'does it leak memory?', 'is it secure?'
  Sell heuristics, never perfection.
example.walkthrough: When a vendor promises perfect behavioral detection, you now know which theorem they're defying.

pitfalls: Despair — undecidability bounds perfection, not usefulness
Ignoring decidable fragments — model checking and types do real work
Promising customers the impossible — the fastest way to lose trust
lessons.try_it: Name one tool you use that's a heuristic recognizer. What's its blind spot?

lessons.title: Alonzo Church and the Lambda Calculus
concepts: Church (Turing's PhD advisor) built lambda calculus in the 1930s: computation as function definition and application — no machines, no tapes
Three constructs: variables (x), abstraction (λx.body — define a function), application (f x — call it)
Everything is a function: numbers, booleans, recursion (via the Y combinator) — a whole computational universe from one idea
Church used it to prove the Entscheidungsproblem unsolvable independently in 1936 — the same answer from a totally different direction

example.code:
Lambda sketches:
  λx.x          identity: returns its input
  λx.x+1        successor (with numbers defined)
  (λx.x) 42  -> 42   application substitutes
Functions all the way down.
example.walkthrough: Two founders, two formalisms, one boundary — that convergence is why we trust the thesis.

pitfalls: Thinking lambda calculus is 'just theory' — it's the ancestor of Lisp, ML, and every functional language
Confusing Church with Turing's student — it was the reverse
Skipping Church — the thesis has two names for a reason
lessons.try_it: Write the identity function and apply it to your name in lambda notation.

lessons.title: Lambda in Ten Minutes
concepts: Beta reduction: (λx.body) arg -> body with arg substituted for x — the single computation rule
Alpha conversion: renaming bound variables (λx.x = λy.y) — names don't matter, structure does
Currying: multi-argument functions are nested single-argument ones — λx.λy.x+y applied as ((f a) b)
Booleans as functions: TRUE = λx.λy.x (pick first), FALSE = λx.λy.y (pick second) — logic from pure functions

example.code:
Beta-reduce (λx.x) 42:
  substitute 42 for x in body 'x'
  -> 42. Done.
Reduce (λx.λy.x) A B:
  -> (λy.A) B -> A. (TRUE picks first!)
example.walkthrough: Do reductions mechanically — substitution is the whole game; intuition follows practice.

pitfalls: Substituting into the wrong scope — bound vs free variables matter (capture!)
Evaluating arguments first always — order can matter; learn normal order
Thinking it's impractical — JavaScript closures are lambda calculus with syntax
lessons.try_it: Beta-reduce these by hand: (λx.x x)(λy.y), (λf.λx.f x) g a.

lessons.title: Equivalence of Models
concepts: Turing machines, lambda calculus, and general recursive functions all define the SAME class of computable functions
Turing proved machines simulate lambda (and Church's students proved the reverse) — the models inter-translate
This robustness is the thesis's evidence: wildly different formalisms, identical boundary — the boundary is real, not an artifact
Practical upshot: pick whichever model suits the proof — machines for lower bounds, lambda for language semantics

example.code:
Equivalence sketch:
  machine -> lambda: encode tape+states as functions
  lambda -> machine: machine performs beta-reduction
  Both directions constructive: translations are programs.
example.walkthrough: When models agree, trust the boundary; when they disagree, you've found an assumption to examine.

pitfalls: 'Equivalent' meaning equally fast — equivalence is about computability, not complexity
Thinking one model is 'truer' — they're notations for one idea
Forgetting partial functions — equivalence covers them too
lessons.try_it: Argue in three sentences why model-equivalence supports the thesis.

lessons.title: The Church-Turing Thesis
concepts: Claim: every effectively calculable function is Turing-computable — 'algorithm' = 'Turing machine program'
It's a THESIS, not a theorem: 'effectively calculable' is an intuitive notion, so no formal proof is possible — only evidence
Evidence: model convergence, 90 years of failed counterexamples, and every physical computer obeying it
Scope: it bounds what algorithms can do, not what physics can do — hypercomputation would need new physics, not new math

example.code:
Thesis vs theorem:
  theorem: proved from axioms
  thesis: empirical claim about an informal notion
  status: unfalsified since 1936
  challengers: must exhibit a physical effective procedure no TM captures
example.walkthrough: Respect the epistemology: the thesis is science's most successful undefeated claim about computation.

pitfalls: Calling it 'proven' — it can't be, by its nature
Stretching it to physics ('the universe is a TM') — that's a stronger, separate claim
Thinking quantum computing refutes it — it doesn't (see next lesson)
lessons.try_it: Explain to a peer why the thesis can't be proved — in your own words.

lessons.title: Beyond Turing? Hypercomputation and Quantum
concepts: Hypercomputation proposals (infinite-time machines, real-number computers) all require physically impossible operations — no evidence, no devices
Quantum computers do NOT compute the uncomputable: they solve certain problems FASTER (factoring, search) — efficiency, not computability
The extended thesis (about efficiency) is what quantum challenges — and that's a live, precise research question
Honest position: thesis stands for computability; efficiency thesis is under active investigation

example.code:
Quantum vs thesis:
  Shor's algorithm: factors fast (efficiency!)
  halting problem: still undecidable on quantum hardware
  verdict: new complexity class (BQP), same computability class
example.walkthrough: Separate 'what can be computed' from 'how fast' — quantum moves the second, not the first.

pitfalls: 'Quantum computers try all answers in parallel' — pop-science myth; it's interference, not parallelism
Assuming faster = more computable — speed never defeats diagonalization
Startup claims of hypercomputation — demand the physical mechanism
lessons.try_it: Write the one-paragraph refutation of 'quantum computers will solve the halting problem.'

lessons.title: Capstone: Turing Machine Simulator — Overview
concepts: Your capstone: a working Turing machine simulator — paper model plus code — that runs real computations, with an essay on the halting problem
Break the build into phases: plan, build, secure, validate, document. Each phase maps to domains in this bootcamp
Document as you go — your write-up is the interview artifact that proves senior-level ownership
Done beats perfect: a working system with honest limitations beats an unfinished ambitious one

example.code:
Phase 1: Design the machine on paper: states, alphabet, transition table
Phase 2: Implement the simulator in code
Phase 3: Run real computations: increment, addition, busy beaver
Phase 4: Write the halting-problem essay in your own words
example.walkthrough: Treat each phase as a mini-project with a definition of done. Demo each phase working before moving on — integration surprises compound.

pitfalls: Starting to build before writing the plan — an hour of planning saves ten of rework
Skipping documentation until the end — you will forget why decisions were made
Gold-plating phase one while phase four remains untouched
lessons.try_it: Write the one-paragraph project plan: what you will build, in what phases, and what 'done' looks like.

lessons.title: Capstone: Validation and Demo
concepts: Validate every requirement with a test you can show: screenshots, command output, or a live demo
Prepare the 5-minute demo narrative: problem, approach, build, validation, lessons learned
Anticipate questions: know the trade-offs you made and what you would do with more time
Publish the write-up: architecture diagram, build log, validation evidence, reflection

example.code:
Demo script template:
  1. The problem (30s)
  2. Architecture overview (60s)
  3. Live walkthrough (2 min)
  4. Validation evidence (60s)
  5. What I would do next (30s)
example.walkthrough: A demo that only shows the happy path invites the hardest questions. Show one failure mode and how the system handles it — that is what interviewers remember.

pitfalls: Demoing without rehearsing — run it three times end-to-end first
Hiding limitations — name them before you are asked
No architecture diagram — draw the system before you demo it
lessons.try_it: Draft your 5-minute demo script for the capstone project.

lessons.title: Hilbert's Program
concepts: Hilbert (1900s-1920s): make mathematics complete (every truth provable), consistent (no contradictions), and decidable (mechanical proof-checking)
Completeness: the dream that axioms capture all mathematical truth — no true statement left unprovable
Consistency: the system must never prove both P and not-P — Hilbert wanted a finitary consistency proof
Decidability: the Entscheidungsproblem — a mechanical procedure settling every mathematical statement

example.code:
Hilbert's three asks:
  1. complete? (prove all truths)
  2. consistent? (prove no contradictions)
  3. decidable? (mechanical procedure)
1931 killed 1&2; 1936 killed 3.
example.walkthrough: Hilbert wasn't naive — his program organized 30 years of logic; its failure was more productive than most successes.

pitfalls: Thinking Hilbert was 'refuted and forgotten' — his questions created the field
Conflating the three goals — each fell to a different theorem
Skipping Hilbert — Turing's paper is incomprehensible without him
lessons.try_it: State Hilbert's three goals in your own words, with one line on each one's fate.

lessons.title: The Entscheidungsproblem
concepts: The decision problem: is there a definite method deciding the truth of any first-order logic statement?
'Definite method' needed a definition — Turing's machine supplied it, making the question answerable
Turing's answer (1936): NO — no such method exists; the proof uses the halting problem's undecidability
Church answered independently via lambda calculus — the convergence that birthed the thesis

example.code:
Entscheidungsproblem, precisely:
  input: a statement in first-order logic
  question: is there an algorithm deciding
            truth for ALL such statements?
  answer: no (Turing 1936, Church 1936)
example.walkthrough: Notice the move: Turing didn't solve the problem — he defined 'method' so precisely the answer became provable.

pitfalls: Thinking it's about decisions in general — it's specifically first-order logic validity
Missing why definition mattered — 'method' was intuitive until the machine formalized it
Forgetting Church — independent convergence again
lessons.try_it: Explain why the Entscheidungsproblem couldn't be answered before 1936.

lessons.title: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems
concepts: First theorem (1931): any consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic contains true but unprovable statements
The Gödel sentence says 'I am unprovable in this system' — true (it IS unprovable) yet unprovable within the system
Second theorem: such a system can't prove its own consistency — killing Hilbert's finitary consistency program
Technique: Gödel numbering — encode statements as numbers so the system talks about itself

example.code:
Gödel sentence G:
  G = 'G is not provable in F'
  if F proves G -> F inconsistent
  if F doesn't -> G is true but unprovable
  Either way, F is incomplete (if consistent).
example.walkthrough: Self-reference isn't a trick — it's the engine. Diagonalization again, wearing number theory.

pitfalls: 'Math is broken' — incompleteness limits formal systems, not mathematical truth
'Everything is relative' — the theorems are precise, not postmodern
Applying Gödel to everything (minds, politics) — the hypotheses rarely transfer
lessons.try_it: Write the Gödel sentence argument in 4 lines from memory.

lessons.title: Formal Systems and Their Limits
concepts: A formal system: axioms + inference rules; proofs are mechanical derivations; truth is semantic (about structures)
Soundness: provable -> true. Completeness: true -> provable. Gödel broke completeness for arithmetic-strength systems
Truth vs provability: truth outruns proof — there are arithmetical truths no axiom system captures
Weaker systems CAN be complete: propositional logic and (surprisingly) Euclidean geometry are decidable

example.code:
Map the territory:
  propositional logic: decidable, complete
  first-order logic: complete, UNDECIDABLE
  arithmetic (PA): incomplete (Gödel)
  Stronger != better behaved.
example.walkthrough: Limits are local: know exactly which system, which property, which theorem.

pitfalls: Overgeneralizing Gödel — it needs arithmetic strength; weak systems escape
Confusing consistency with truth — related, not identical
Thinking incompleteness stops math — mathematicians prove theorems daily; they just can't formalize ALL truth
lessons.try_it: Place three systems you know on the decidable/complete map.

lessons.title: From Logic to Machines
concepts: The pipeline: Hilbert asks -> Gödel limits proof -> Turing defines computation -> the computer is born from the wreckage
Logic's failure was CS's foundation: the precise definition of 'method' became the blueprint for programming
Undecidability results ARE computer science results — every 'impossible' in CS descends from 1931/1936
Lesson: foundational crises are productive — the rubble of Hilbert's program built an industry

example.code:
Causal chain:
  Entscheidungsproblem
    -> define 'method' (TM)
    -> universal machine
    -> stored program
    -> actual computers
  Philosophy -> engineering.
example.walkthrough: When theory seems 'useless,' remember: the most practical object in history came from a logic problem.

pitfalls: Treating history as trivia — the causal chain explains WHY computers look this way
Separating 'theory' from 'practice' — here they're one story
Missing the pattern — today's 'useless' theory is tomorrow's infrastructure
lessons.try_it: Draw the Hilbert-to-computer causal chain with dates.

lessons.title: 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950)
concepts: Opens by replacing 'can machines think?' with the imitation game — refusing the vague question, substituting an operational test
Structure: the game, nine objections (theological to ESP) with replies, then learning machines and predictions
Written for the general reader — witty, clear, philosophical; the rare foundational paper that's actually enjoyable
The paper's move is methodological: intelligence as an empirical question, not a metaphysical one

example.code:
Paper map:
  1. The imitation game (operational test)
  2. Nine objections + replies
  3. Learning machines (the child machine)
  4. Predictions
Read it in order — it builds.
example.walkthrough: Read the original before the commentaries — most 'Turing test' discourse describes a test Turing didn't propose.

pitfalls: Skipping to the objections — the game's setup justifies everything after
Reading modern summaries only — the wit carries the argument
Treating it as a prediction paper — it's primarily methodological
lessons.try_it: Read section 1 of the 1950 paper. Summarize the game setup in 3 sentences.

lessons.title: The Imitation Game
concepts: Actual setup: an interrogator converses via text with a human and a machine, trying to tell which is which — originally a man/woman imitation variant too
Turing's prediction: by 2000, machines with 1GB storage would fool interrogators 30% of the time after 5 minutes
The test is about BEHAVIOR under constrained interaction — not consciousness, not understanding, not inner life
Pop version ('chatbot fools a judge') drops the controls: time limits, the human baseline, and what 'fooling' rates mean

example.code:
Game spec:
  players: interrogator, human, machine
  channel: text only (no voice/appearance)
  task: identify the machine
  bar: 30% misidentification, 5 min, by 2000
Controls matter — they're the science.
example.walkthrough: When evaluating any 'Turing test passed' headline, check the controls first: time, baseline, misidentification rate.

pitfalls: The 'fooling' framing — it's misidentification rate, not deception skill
Ignoring the human baseline — humans fail too, which calibrates the bar
One-off demos as 'passing' — the prediction was statistical
lessons.try_it: Design a 5-minute imitation protocol with proper controls. What's hardest to control?

lessons.title: Turing on Learning Machines
concepts: The child machine: instead of programming adult intelligence, simulate a child's mind and EDUCATE it — training before 'training' was a field
Proposed ingredients: initial structure, education (experience), and random mutation/selection — strikingly evolutionary
'An important feature of a learning machine is that its teacher will often be very largely ignorant of quite what is going on inside'
This is 1950 describing, in prose, the paradigm that would become machine learning decades later

example.code:
Child machine recipe (1950):
  1. build a simple learning substrate
  2. educate via experience (rewards/punishments)
  3. allow mutation + selection
  4. teacher won't fully understand the inside
Sound familiar? It should.
example.walkthrough: Turing bet on learning over programming — the field took 60 years to agree with him.

pitfalls: 'Turing invented ML' — he sketched the paradigm; the engineering came later
Skipping this section — it's the paper's most prescient part
Thinking education means datasets only — Turing meant interaction
lessons.try_it: List three modern ML practices prefigured in the learning-machines section.

lessons.title: Objections and Turing's Replies
concepts: Theological ('thinking is a soul's function'): Turing notes the question applies equally to humans — and declines theology as a test criterion
Mathematical (Gödel limits): yes, machines have limits — but so do humans facing the same formal limits; the objection proves too much
Consciousness ('no machine feels'): Turing's behaviorist shrug — we infer other minds from behavior; apply the same standard
Lady Lovelace ('machines can't originate'): machines can surprise us — programmers routinely don't foresee outputs; learning machines doubly so

example.code:
Reply pattern:
  objection: machines lack X
  Turing: (a) humans face the same formal limit, or
           (b) X is untestable, use behavior, or
           (c) learning machines change the premise
  Learn the three moves.
example.walkthrough: Turing rarely 'wins' outright — he dissolves bad questions and reframes the rest. That's the skill to steal.

pitfalls: Treating replies as knockouts — they're reframings, study the move not the score
Skipping to your favorite objection — the set is the argument
Missing the Lovelace reply's depth — surprise vs origination is still debated
lessons.try_it: Pick one objection; steelman it, then give Turing's reply in your words.

lessons.title: What Turing Got Right (and Wrong)
concepts: Right: learning over programming, behavioral/operational framing, the 1GB-by-2000 storage guess (roughly correct!), chess as AI's drosophila
Wrong-ish: the 30%-in-5-minutes bar proved easier to game than meaningful — modern LLMs 'pass' thin versions without settling anything
Unresolved: whether imitation captures intelligence — the field split into capabilities research (his heirs) and understanding research (his critics)
Honest score: methodology A+, specific predictions B — the frame outlasted the forecast

example.code:
Scorecard:
  learning paradigm: A (prescient)
  operational test: A- (framed the field)
  1GB by 2000: B+ (close!)
  30% bar: C (gameable)
  chess focus: A (still central)
Grade predictions, keep methods.
example.walkthrough: Separate the methodology (durable) from the predictions (perishable) — in all visionary papers, not just this one.

pitfalls: 'Turing predicted ChatGPT' — he predicted the paradigm, not the product
Dismissing the test because chatbots exist — the controls were the point
Treating 1950 as scripture — update with 75 years of evidence
lessons.try_it: Write your own 2-paragraph scorecard of one more Turing prediction.

lessons.title: The Enigma Machine
concepts: Rotors: 3-5 wired wheels; each keypress advances the first, with turnover notches cascading — 17,576+ starting positions
Reflector: sends current back through rotors — same setting encrypts AND decrypts, but no letter ever encrypts to itself
Plugboard (Stecker): swaps letter pairs before/after rotors — the setting the Poles couldn't solve alone, 150M+ combinations
Why it seemed unbreakable: astronomical keyspace — the flaw was never the math, it was the procedures

example.code:
Keyspace sketch:
  rotors: 3 of 5 -> 60 orders
  positions: 26^3 = 17,576
  plugboard: ~150,000,000,000
  total: ~10^23 — brute force: no.
  Procedure flaws: yes.
example.walkthrough: Security lives in procedure, not just keyspace — Enigma is the canonical demonstration.

pitfalls: 'Unbreakable math' — the math held; humans leaked
Ignoring the reflector's gift — no-self-encryption enabled cribs
Forgetting the plugboard — it was the late, hard addition
lessons.try_it: Compute 26^3 by hand. Feel why brute force was hopeless in 1940.

lessons.title: Keys, Codebooks, and Daily Procedure
concepts: Daily key: rotor order, ring settings, plugboard pairs — distributed in codebooks, changed at midnight
Operators chose message keys (3 letters) and transmitted them TWICE, encrypted — the repetition the Poles exploited
Cillies: lazy operators reused keys ('CIL' = girlfriend's initials) — human randomness fails predictably
Lesson: the system was attacked at its weakest link — never the rotor wiring, always the humans and procedures

example.code:
Attack surface, ranked:
  1. operator habits (cillies, repeats)
  2. procedure (doubled message keys)
  3. key distribution (captured codebooks)
  4. machine math (never broken)
Attack humans first.
example.walkthrough: Every 'unbreakable' system in your career will have a cillie equivalent — find it.

pitfalls: Blaming the machine — it did its job
Assuming modern systems lack cillies — defaults and reuse persist
Ignoring key distribution — the hardest problem in crypto, then and now
lessons.try_it: List three modern 'cillies' (human weak links in strong systems).

lessons.title: Bletchley Park and Hut 8
concepts: Turing arrived September 1939; Hut 8 handled naval Enigma — the hardest, most valuable traffic (U-boats)
Organization: huts by problem, 24/7 shifts, thousands of staff (mostly women) — industrial cryptanalysis
Turing's style: mathematical attacks (Banburismus) plus engineering (Bombe spec) — theory to machine
Naval Enigma's extra rotors and procedures made it the supreme challenge — breaking it saved convoys, measurably

example.code:
Hut 8 pipeline:
  intercepts -> cribs (guessed plaintext)
  -> Banburismus (rotor order odds)
  -> Bombe (plugboard + positions)
  -> human check -> intelligence
  Math -> machine -> humans.
example.walkthrough: Industrial scale matters: brilliance organized beats brilliance alone — Bletchley was a factory.

pitfalls: 'Turing single-handedly' — Hut 8 was a team; credit Welchman, Alexander, the Wrens
Forgetting the operators — the Y-service interceptors made it all possible
Movie history — verify against Hinsley, Hodges, Copeland
lessons.try_it: Name three Hut 8 contributors besides Turing and one contribution each.

lessons.title: The Bombe
concepts: Purpose: find the daily key — given a crib (guessed plaintext), search rotor positions and plugboard settings mechanically
Turing's insight: the crib creates LOOPS of logical constraints; the Bombe tests positions where all loop constraints hold simultaneously
Welchman's diagonal board multiplied its power — the Bombe was a collaboration, Turing's spec plus Welchman's enhancement
36+ Bombes ran around the clock — electromechanical brute force guided by mathematical constraints

example.code:
Bombe logic:
  crib: plaintext P aligns with cipher C
  loop: P1->C1->P2->C2->P1 (plugboard links)
  test each rotor position:
    position valid iff loop is consistent
  Consistency prunes 10^23 to checkable.
example.walkthrough: Constraints beat brute force: the Bombe searched smart, not just fast.

pitfalls: 'The Bombe decrypted messages' — it found KEYS; humans decrypted
Crediting Turing alone — Welchman's diagonal board was decisive
Confusing with Colossus — different machine, different cipher (Tunny)
lessons.try_it: Draw a 3-letter crib loop and explain why inconsistency kills positions.

lessons.title: Banburismus and Beyond
concepts: Banburismus: Turing's statistical method — scoring rotor-order hypotheses using letter-frequency coincidences on punched Banbury sheets
Bayesian before Bayesian was cool: accumulate weak evidence (bigram scores) until one hypothesis dominates — sequential analysis
It cut Bombe time dramatically by ordering rotor orders by likelihood — statistics guiding search
Legacy: the first large-scale Bayesian cryptanalysis — ancestor of modern statistical methods everywhere

example.code:
Banburismus essence:
  compare intercepted bigrams vs cribs
  score coincidences (Banbury sheets)
  accumulate log-odds per rotor order
  try orders best-first on the Bombe
  Weak evidence, added up, becomes strong.
example.walkthrough: When brute force is impossible, rank hypotheses statistically and search best-first — still the playbook.

pitfalls: Dismissing it as 'just statistics' — it was the mathematical core of Hut 8's speed
Thinking Bayes is modern — Turing did sequential Bayes by hand in 1940
Skipping it — Banburismus shows Turing the statistician, not just the logician
lessons.try_it: Explain in two sentences how weak evidence becomes decisive when accumulated.

lessons.title: From Wartime Ciphers to Modern Crypto
concepts: Arc: rotor machines (Enigma) -> DES (1970s, 56-bit) -> RSA (1977, public key) -> AES (2001, the standard)
Kerckhoffs's principle: security must rest in the KEY, not the algorithm's secrecy — Enigma's lesson, formalized
Computational security replaced 'unbreakable' claims: 'breaking costs more than the secret is worth'
Turing's bridge: statistical cryptanalysis (Banburismus) became the mathematical mainstream of the field

example.code:
Crypto eras:
  mechanical (rotors) ->
  symmetric digital (DES/AES) ->
  public-key (RSA/ECC) ->
  post-quantum (in progress)
Each era: new math, same principles.
example.walkthrough: History isn't nostalgia — every modern principle (Kerckhoffs, key distribution, side channels) was learned the hard way first.

pitfalls: 'Modern crypto made history irrelevant' — the principles ARE the history
Trusting 'military-grade' marketing — Kerckhoffs applies to vendors too
Ignoring the pre-computer era — rotor lessons recur in IoT ciphers
lessons.try_it: Name one modern system violating Kerckhoffs's principle (secret algorithm). What should it do?

lessons.title: The One-Time Pad: Perfect and Impractical
concepts: Shannon (1949): OTP has perfect secrecy — cipher reveals ZERO information about plaintext, provably
Requirements: key truly random, as long as the message, never reused — violate any and security collapses
The catch: key DISTRIBUTION — securely sharing a key as long as the message is as hard as the original problem
Use cases: ultra-high-value, low-volume (hotlines, spies) — never general purpose

example.code:
OTP encrypt HELLO:
  key (random):  XMCKL
  H+X, E+M, L+C, L+K, O+L (mod 26)
  -> cipher. Decrypt: subtract key.
  Reuse the key once -> breakable.
example.walkthrough: Perfect secrecy is real and useless at scale — the lesson is about trade-offs, not magic.

pitfalls: 'Unbreakable encryption!' marketing — ask about the key management
Reusing pads — the Venona story: Soviet reuse broke 'unbreakable'
Pseudorandom keys — OTP needs TRUE randomness
lessons.try_it: Encrypt your name with a coin-flip key. Then reuse the key — see what leaks.

lessons.title: Turing's Delilah
concepts: Delilah: Turing's postwar portable voice-encryption system — speech scrambled for secure field communication
Built at Hanslope Park/MI6 orbit after Bletchley; never used operationally, but the engineering was real
Shows Turing the engineer: not just theory — building working secure-voice hardware
Legacy: early spread-spectrum/secure-voice ideas — the problems (sync, keying, bandwidth) persist today

example.code:
Delilah's problem set:
  scramble voice -> unintelligible
  authorized receiver -> descramble
  constraints: portable, real-time,
  1940s electronics
Same problems as modern secure voice.
example.walkthrough: Don't reduce Turing to 1936+1950 — the engineering years matter.

pitfalls: 'Turing only did theory' — Delilah, the Bombe spec, ACE say otherwise
Confusing Delilah with Enigma work — postwar, different problem
Overclaiming its impact — honest: brilliant, unused, instructive
lessons.try_it: List the engineering constraints secure voice still faces today.

lessons.title: The Public-Key Revolution
concepts: The key-distribution problem: symmetric crypto needs shared secrets — sharing them securely at scale was THE blocker
Diffie-Hellman (1976): exchange keys over public channels using discrete-log hardness — the conceptual earthquake
RSA (1977): public encryption + digital signatures from factoring hardness — GCHQ had it earlier (Ellis, secret)
What it solved: strangers can communicate securely with no prior shared secret — the internet's enabling trick

example.code:
DH intuition:
  public: paint-mixing is easy,
  unmixing is hard
  Alice+Bob mix public+secret colors
  shared secret emerges; observers can't
  (discrete logs, really — but feel it)
example.walkthrough: Every 'https://' handshake is the revolution working — key distribution solved in the open.

pitfalls: 'Public key means no secrets' — private keys are very secret
Ignoring the GCHQ prehistory — Ellis/Cocks/Williams, classified
Thinking RSA is forever — quantum threatens factoring; migrate
lessons.try_it: Explain DH to a peer using the paint analogy, then state the real math.

lessons.title: Turing's Cryptographic Legacy
concepts: Statistical cryptanalysis: Banburismus scored hypotheses with accumulated weak evidence — the Bayesian method in action
Modern heirs: spam filters, intrusion detection, side-channel analysis — all accumulate weak signals into strong verdicts
Crib-dragging -> known-plaintext attacks: the reflector lesson generalized — structural constraints are attack surface
Meta-lesson: attack the system as deployed (procedures, humans, side channels), never just the math

example.code:
Turing's crypto playbook:
  1. find the procedural flaw
  2. get a crib (known plaintext)
  3. score hypotheses statistically
  4. mechanize the search
  Still the playbook. Still winning.
example.walkthrough: When evaluating any crypto product, run Turing's playbook against it mentally.

pitfalls: Math-only security analysis — the playbook says look wider
Forgetting side channels — timing, power, errors leak
Underestimating statistics — weak signals add up
lessons.try_it: Apply the 4-step playbook to a messaging app you use. Where's the weak link?

lessons.title: The Test as Specified
concepts: Setup: interrogator, human, machine — text-only channel; interrogator identifies the machine
Turing's numbers: by 2000, 1GB machines would achieve 30% misidentification after 5 minutes
The original paper ALSO describes a man/woman imitation variant — the game generalizes beyond machines
Misidentification rate, not 'fooling': the statistic is judges wrong, not machines clever

example.code:
Spec checklist:
  text-only channel
  human baseline present
  fixed time (5 min)
  misidentification rate (30%)
  statistical, not anecdotal
Missing any -> not the test.
example.walkthrough: Judge every 'passed the Turing test' headline against this checklist first.

pitfalls: The chatbot-fools-judge pop version — no controls, no baseline
'Fooling' as deception skill — it's a rate statistic
Ignoring the gender-imitation variant — it shows the game's generality
lessons.try_it: Write the 5-line spec from memory. Then check a recent headline against it.

lessons.title: What Passing Would and Wouldn't Prove
concepts: Would prove: behaviorally indistinguishable performance under the specified conditions — a real, bounded achievement
Wouldn't prove: consciousness, understanding, inner experience — the test is behaviorist by design
Sufficient, not necessary: failing doesn't prove unintelligence (a shy genius fails); passing doesn't prove mind
Turing's framing: the test replaces an unanswerable question with an answerable one — that's the contribution

example.code:
Logic of the test:
  pass -> behaves intelligently (under conditions)
  pass -/-> is conscious
  fail -/-> is unintelligent
  The arrows matter more than the verdict.
example.walkthrough: Keep the logic straight and most 'test' debates dissolve into agreements.

pitfalls: Pass = conscious — the test never claimed this
Fail = stupid — sufficient, not necessary
Demanding the test settle philosophy — it was built to sidestep it
lessons.try_it: Draw the three arrows (pass/fail vs conscious/intelligent) correctly.

lessons.title: Searle's Chinese Room
concepts: Setup (1980): a man in a room manipulates Chinese symbols by rulebook — outputs perfect Chinese, understands none
Searle's claim: syntax isn't semantics — running the right program doesn't create understanding
Systems reply: the MAN doesn't understand, but the SYSTEM (man + rulebook + room) might — understanding is a system property
Status: unresolved after 40+ years — it clarified the question (what would understanding BE?) more than settling it

example.code:
The dialectic:
  Searle: rule-following != understanding
  systems reply: the room understands
  Searle: internalize it all — still no understanding
  ...and the field learned to ask better questions
example.walkthrough: Steelman before you rebut — Searle's argument deserves its strongest form first.

pitfalls: Strawmanning Searle — engage the systems reply seriously
Thinking it 'refutes AI' — it targets a specific claim about programs
Skipping it — the debate shaped cognitive science
lessons.try_it: Write Searle's argument in 5 lines, then the systems reply in 3.

lessons.title: Modern Evaluation: Beyond the Imitation Game
concepts: Problem: benchmarks saturate, models train on test data (contamination), and 'vibes' aren't measurement
Capability evals: test what systems CAN do (reasoning, tool use, deception) with held-out, adversarial tasks
The field moved from 'is it intelligent?' to 'what can it do, reliably, and where does it fail?' — Turing would approve of the operationalism
Honest eval needs: held-out data, baselines, error analysis, and pre-registered protocols

example.code:
Eval checklist:
  held-out test data (no contamination)
  human + trivial baselines
  adversarial cases, not just typical
  failure analysis, not just scores
  protocol pre-registered
example.walkthrough: If you can't say how it fails, you haven't evaluated it — you've advertised it.

pitfalls: Benchmark scores as intelligence — Goodhart's law eats benchmarks
Ignoring contamination — trained-on-test is the open secret
No baselines — 80% means nothing without them
lessons.try_it: Take one benchmark you trust; check it against the 5-line checklist.

lessons.title: The Test's Real Legacy
concepts: Operational definitions: replace foggy questions with testable ones — the method outlived the specific test
The field's founding provocation: AI organized itself around (and against) the imitation game for decades
CAPTCHAs are the inverted Turing test — machines testing humans — a billion daily deployments of the idea
Legacy verdict: the frame (empirical, behavioral, statistical) beat the forecast (30% by 2000)

example.code:
Legacy inventory:
  operationalism -> all of AI eval
  imitation game -> chatbot benchmarks
  inverted test -> CAPTCHAs
  behavioral framing -> cognitive science debates
The idea compound-interest'd.
example.walkthrough: When a specific prediction fails but the method spreads, the method was the contribution.

pitfalls: Remembering only the test, not the method
Missing CAPTCHAs — the test's mass deployment
Treating 1950 as the end — it was the opening move
lessons.try_it: Name one modern practice that IS operationalism, Turing-style.

lessons.title: Tunny and the Lorenz Cipher
concepts: Lorenz SZ40/42: 12 wheels encrypting 5-bit teleprinter code — Hitler's high-command traffic, far harder than Enigma
Keyspace dwarfed Enigma's; no crib-friendly reflector flaw; operator discipline was better
The break came from a MISTAKE: an operator re-sent a 4000-character message with the same key (a 'depth') — Tutte exploited it
Tunny traffic was the most valuable intelligence of the war — strategic, not tactical

example.code:
Tunny vs Enigma:
  Enigma: 3-5 rotors, letters, reflector flaw
  Tunny: 12 wheels, 5-bit code, no such flaw
  break: operator depth + Tutte's statistics
  value: high-command strategy
Harder machine, bigger prize.
example.walkthrough: Depths kill: key reuse is the original sin of stream ciphers — then and now.

pitfalls: 'Enigma was the hard one' — Tunny was harder and more valuable
Confusing Tunny with Enigma — different machines, different breaks
Missing the depth — the whole break started with one lazy retransmission
lessons.try_it: Explain in two sentences how a 'depth' breaks a stream cipher.

lessons.title: Colossus
concepts: Built by Tommy Flowers (Post Office engineer) 1943-44: electronic, programmable-ish, built to run Tutte's statistical attack on Tunny
1,500-2,400 valves (tubes) — when 'experts' said valves couldn't be reliable at scale; Flowers proved them wrong
What it did: counted statistical coincidences at electronic speed — mechanized cryptanalysis, not a stored-program computer
First large-scale electronic digital computer — operational before ENIAC, but classified into obscurity

example.code:
Colossus essence:
  input: intercepted Tunny stream (paper tape)
  method: Tutte's statistics, electronic speed
  output: wheel settings -> decrypts
  NOT: general-purpose, stored-program
Special-purpose, world-changing.
example.walkthrough: Flowers bet his career on valves against expert consensus — engineering courage as a historical force.

pitfalls: 'Colossus was the first computer' — first ELECTRONIC digital; not general-purpose/stored-program
Crediting Turing with building it — Flowers built it; Turing consulted
Confusing with the Bombe — Tunny vs Enigma, always
lessons.try_it: State precisely what Colossus was and wasn't, in 3 lines.

lessons.title: Newmanry and the Testery
concepts: Max Newman's section mechanized Tunny-breaking; the Testery (Tiltman, Tutte) did it by hand first — machines followed methods
Bill Tutte, 24, deduced the Lorenz machine's ENTIRE logical structure from a single 4000-char depth — no machine seen, pure inference
Turing's role: consultant — key ideas (including 'Turingery,' a wheel-breaking method), not day-to-day leadership
Pipeline: Tutte's statistics -> Flowers's electronics -> Newmanry's industrial operation

example.code:
Credit map:
  Tiltman: spotted the depth
  Tutte: reverse-engineered Lorenz blind
  Flowers: built Colossus
  Newman: ran the section
  Turing: consulting breakthroughs
Teams, not lone geniuses.
example.walkthrough: Methods before machines: the Testery proved it by hand, then mechanized — automate the proven, not the hoped.

pitfalls: 'Turing built Colossus' — the most common error; Flowers did
Skipping Tutte — the deepest single cryptanalytic feat of the war
Forgetting the Testery — hand methods validated the machine
lessons.try_it: Summarize Tutte's feat in two sentences — no machine, just a depth.

lessons.title: From Bletchley to ACE
concepts: 1945: Turing's ACE proposal at NPL — among the first complete stored-program computer designs, with subroutines and a terse instruction set
Wartime lessons in ACE: electronics are reliable (Flowers proved it), programs belong in memory (UTM, 1936), design for speed
NPL delays and politics slowed ACE; the Pilot ACE ran in 1950 — fast, influential, late
Lineage: Bletchley's engineering culture -> ACE -> British computing — the war built the peacetime industry

example.code:
ACE innovations:
  stored program (UTM made real)
  subroutines as first-class
  minimal instruction set, maximum speed
  'building' the 1936 paper, 1945-style
example.walkthrough: Ideas become machines when the engineering culture exists — Bletchley was the culture.

pitfalls: 'ACE was never built' — Pilot ACE ran 1950, among the fastest
Skipping the politics — delays were human, not technical
Isolating ACE from Bletchley — the lineage is the lesson
lessons.try_it: Trace one ACE feature back to a wartime lesson.

lessons.title: Secrecy and Its Cost
concepts: Colossus stayed classified into the 1970s; most machines were destroyed — the official history of computing was written without it
Cost: Flowers got little credit or funding; Britain's computing lead narrative went to America; pioneers died unrecognized
Turing's war work stayed secret through his 1952 prosecution — the state he saved wouldn't acknowledge what he'd done
Lesson: secrecy has compound interest — decades of lost credit, lost funding, lost history

example.code:
Secrecy's bill:
  Flowers: no recognition, no capital
  Britain: lost narrative, lost momentum
  Turing: secret service at his trial
  computing: distorted origin story
Paid for decades.
example.walkthrough: Classify carefully — but count the cost honestly. Secrecy isn't free.

pitfalls: 'Secrecy was necessary so it was fine' — necessary AND costly; both true
Forgetting the human cost — recognition is a real human need
Assuming declassification fixed it — narratives set early are sticky
lessons.try_it: Name one concrete thing secrecy cost a Bletchley figure.

lessons.title: ACE and Pilot ACE
concepts: 1945: Turing's ACE report at NPL — among the first complete stored-program designs, with subroutines and minimal instructions
Design philosophy: hardware minimal, software maximal — push complexity into code, keep the machine fast and simple
NPL bureaucracy + Turing's impatience = delays; the Pilot ACE ran May 1950, among the world's fastest then
Influence: ACE ideas fed British computing (including the Elliott/Bendix lines) — the design outran its administration

example.code:
ACE in one line:
  minimal hardware + subroutines +
  stored program + blinding speed
  = the 1936 UTM, engineered 1945.
Theory, finally built.
example.walkthrough: Brilliant designs need organizational luck too — ACE's lesson is institutional, not just technical.

pitfalls: 'ACE failed' — Pilot ACE ran and was fast; the project was delayed, not dead
Skipping the NPL politics — they explain the timeline
Isolating ACE from Bletchley — wartime culture built it
lessons.try_it: Name two ACE innovations and their modern descendants.

lessons.title: Morphogenesis: Patterns from Chemistry
concepts: 1952 paper 'The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis': how uniform chemistry produces spots, stripes, segments
Reaction-diffusion: an activator spreads slowly + inhibitor spreads fast = spontaneous pattern from uniformity
Worked example: leopard spots, zebra stripes, digit formation — symmetry breaking from noise
Legacy: mathematical biology's founding text; confirmed in living systems decades later (2012+ mouse/tooth experiments)

example.code:
Reaction-diffusion intuition:
  activator: makes more of itself, diffuses SLOW
  inhibitor: suppresses activator, diffuses FAST
  result: spots! (local activation wins nearby,
  inhibition wins at distance)
example.walkthrough: Uniformity + local rules -> global pattern: the deepest idea in self-organization, from a logician.

pitfalls: 'Turing dabbled in biology' — it founded mathematical biology
Skipping the math — the instability analysis IS the paper
Thinking patterns need blueprints — no, they self-organize
lessons.try_it: Explain spots-vs-stripes in reaction-diffusion terms, two sentences.

lessons.title: The Turing Award
concepts: ACM's award since 1966 — computing's Nobel: ~$1M prize, the field's highest honor
Named for Turing because the field's foundations ARE his: computability, the universal machine, AI
Laureates map the field's history: Dijkstra, Knuth, Thompson/Ritchie, Hinton/LeCun/Bengio — read the list as a syllabus
Use it as a curriculum: each laureate's work connects back to something in this bootcamp

example.code:
Award as syllabus:
  Dijkstra -> algorithms
  Thompson/Ritchie -> systems (UTM's heirs)
  Diffie/Hellman -> crypto chapter
  Hinton et al. -> learning machines
One list, the whole field.
example.walkthrough: Prizes follow foundations — the award's existence is itself a statement about who built the field.

pitfalls: Treating it as trivia — it's a map of the discipline
Only knowing recent winners — the early ones defined the terms
Missing the naming point — the field named its Nobel for HIM
lessons.try_it: Pick one laureate; connect their work to a Turing idea from this course.

lessons.title: Persecution, Apology, Pardon
concepts: 1952: prosecuted for homosexuality (then criminal in Britain); sentenced to chemical castration; security clearance revoked
1954: died at 41 — the state he'd served wouldn't acknowledge his war work at his trial
2009: Prime Minister's apology; 2013: royal pardon; 2017: 'Alan Turing law' pardoning others convicted under the same law
Teach it plainly: the injustice is fact, the loss is incalculable — and Britain's eventual reckoning was decades late

example.code:
Timeline of justice:
  1952 prosecution
  1954 death
  2009 apology (55 years)
  2013 pardon
  2017 Alan Turing law
Late is the honest word.
example.walkthrough: Lead with the work, include the injustice fully — he was a genius who was wronged.

pitfalls: Sensationalizing — the facts are damning enough
Skipping it — the story is incomplete without it
Presentism without context — 1952 Britain, stated plainly, judged honestly
lessons.try_it: State the 1952-2017 timeline from memory, with the key legal terms.

lessons.title: Turing's Living Legacy
concepts: AI: the imitation game -> modern eval; learning machines -> deep learning's paradigm
Crypto: statistical methods -> Bayesian security; Kerckhoffs's world -> his wartime lessons
Theory: computability -> complexity (P vs NP is asked in his language); the thesis still undefeated
Culture: the £50 note (2021), the award, the law bearing his name — the rare scientist on currency

example.code:
Legacy audit:
  your interpreter: UTM
  your linter's limits: undecidability
  your spam filter: Banburismus
  your chatbot eval: imitation game
  your banknote (UK): his face
Count them daily.
example.walkthrough: The test of a legacy: how much of the modern world silently runs on it.

pitfalls: Confining him to history — he's infrastructure
The note as trivia — currency is a civilization's honor roll
Forgetting morphogenesis — biology, not just computing
lessons.try_it: Find three Turing ideas running silently in your daily tools.

lessons.title: Turing in One Hour: The Arc of a Life
concepts: 1912 born London; 1936 the computable-numbers paper (age 24); 1939-45 Bletchley Park — Hut 8, the Bombe, Banburismus
1945-47 the ACE design at NPL; 1948 Manchester — programming, morphogenesis beginnings; 1950 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence'; 1952 the morphogenesis paper
1952 prosecution for homosexuality, then a crime in Britain; chemical castration ordered by the court; 1954 death at 41
2009 government apology, 2013 royal pardon, 2017 the 'Alan Turing law' — recognition took longer than his life

example.code:
Arc in four beats:
  logic (1936) -> war (1939-45) ->
  machines (1945-50) -> mind & nature (1950-54)
Each beat built on the last.
example.walkthrough: The arc isn't tragedy-first: lead with the ideas, then the injustice — he was a genius who was wronged, not a victim who did math.

pitfalls: Compressing Bletchley to 'he cracked Enigma alone' — hundreds contributed; Turing's role was real but specific
Getting dates wrong — 1936/1950/1952/1954 anchor everything
Skipping Manchester — ACE, morphogenesis, and early programming matter
lessons.try_it: Place these on a timeline from memory: 1936 paper, Bletchley, ACE, 1950 paper, morphogenesis, pardon.

lessons.title: Why Turing Matters to Every Programmer
concepts: Stored program: your code and data share memory — the universal machine's tape, engineered
Computability: 'can this be automated?' has a principled answer — Rice's theorem prices every analysis tool
AI: the imitation game framed machine intelligence as an empirical question, not a mystical one
Crypto and statistics: Banburismus-style Bayesian scoring lives on in spam filters and cryptanalysis

example.code:
Daily Turing inventory:
  interpreter/VM -> universal machine
  linter limits -> undecidability
  chatbot eval -> imitation game
  Bayesian filter -> Banburismus
Find one per day for a week.
example.walkthrough: You don't need to cite him — you need to recognize when you're standing on his ideas.

pitfalls: Name-dropping without understanding — worse than silence
Thinking theory is 'academic' — your tools' limits are his theorems
Only knowing the biography — the ideas are the legacy
lessons.try_it: Pick one tool you use daily; name the Turing idea inside it.

lessons.title: How to Read Turing's Original Papers
concepts: 1936 'On Computable Numbers': read sections 1-2 (the machine), 6 (universal), 8 (undecidability) — skip the computable-numbers machinery on first pass
1950 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence': read straight through — it's written for a general educated audience, witty and clear
1952 morphogenesis: skim the chemistry, study the instability argument — pattern from uniform beginnings
Reading rule: first pass for the argument's shape, second for details, third with pencil proving each step

example.code:
Reading order:
  1. 1950 paper (accessible, fun)
  2. 1936 sections 1,2,6,8 (the core)
  3. 1952 (the surprise)
  Pencil mandatory from step 2.
example.walkthrough: Turing wrote clearly — difficulty is in the ideas, not the prose. Trust the text.

pitfalls: Reading 1936 linearly cover-to-cover first — you'll drown in computable reals
Skipping the proofs — the argument IS the proof
Modernized summaries only — the originals repay the effort
lessons.try_it: Read the first 3 pages of the 1950 paper tonight. Note one surprise.

lessons.title: The Turing Mindset: From Puzzles to Principles
concepts: Operational definitions: don't ask 'can machines think?' — ask 'what would we observe if they could?' Replace fog with tests
Impossibility as discovery: proving something CAN'T be done is a result, not a failure — it maps the territory
Build the minimal model: strip a question to its essence (the machine), prove things there, then generalize
Fearless range: logic, cryptanalysis, engineering, philosophy, biology — follow the problem, not the discipline

example.code:
Mindset checklist:
  define it so you could test it
  find the minimal model
  ask what's impossible, not just what's hard
  follow the problem across fields
example.walkthrough: Apply the checklist to your hardest current problem — where's the fog?

pitfalls: Mystery-mongering — 'consciousness is ineffable' ends inquiry; Turing operationalized
Discipline loyalty — the best tool may live in another field
Fearing negative results — 'impossible' is information
lessons.try_it: Take one vague question you care about; operationalize it Turing-style.

labs.title: Build a working Turing machine
labs.objective: Implement a Turing machine simulator and run a binary incrementer on it, connecting the 1936 abstraction to executable code.
steps: Write a Python function step(tape, head, state, table) that applies one transition rule from a state table.
Encode the binary-incrementer state table: in state 'carry', reading 1 writes 0 and moves left; reading 0 writes 1 and halts; reading blank writes 1 and halts.
Run the simulator on the tape '1011' and print the final tape.
Test it on '1111' (expect '10000') and '0' (expect '1').
Write a one-paragraph note: what does the universal machine add on top of this single-purpose machine?

checks.hint: Your simulator should turn the tape 1111 into 10000 — the carry must propagate past the left end.

labs.title: Feel the halting problem
labs.objective: Construct the diagonal argument as code: build a program that contradicts any claimed halting decider, and see why the universal claim collapses.
steps: Write a function halts_claim(program, inp) that pretends to be a decider — have it return True for two sample programs and False for an obvious infinite loop.
Write a program diagonal(src) that calls halts_claim on its own source: if the claim says it halts, loop forever; otherwise return immediately.
Trace by hand what happens when halts_claim is asked about diagonal — write down the contradiction for both possible answers.
Generalize in one paragraph: why does this refute EVERY candidate decider, not just your stub?
List two real tools (e.g., linters, model checkers) and state the restriction each accepts to stay useful despite undecidability.

checks.hint: Print the word 'contradiction' from your trace for each of the decider's two possible answers.

labs.title: Hand-Trace the Incrementer
labs.objective: Trace the binary incrementer on paper until the mechanics are automatic.
steps: Draw the 6 transition rules for the binary incrementer
Trace input 1011 by hand, marking head position each step; verify 1100
Trace 111 (expect 1000 — the blank-to-1 rule matters)
Write one paragraph: what the trace taught you about 'algorithm'

checks.hint: The all-ones case exercises the blank rule

labs.success_message: You can now execute a Turing machine like hardware — the model is in your hands.

labs.title: State Table for Unary Addition
labs.objective: Design a complete transition table that adds two unary numbers.
steps: Represent numbers as blocks of 1s separated by a blank: 111_11 means 3+2
Design states: find the separator, erase it, clean up, halt
Write every (state, symbol) rule — no gaps; decide what each undefined combo does
Trace 11_111 by hand; verify the tape shows 11111

checks.hint: Every state-symbol pair needs a rule

labs.success_message: You've designed a real computation from nothing but states and rules.

labs.title: Build a TM Simulator in Python
labs.objective: Implement a universal-style simulator and run real machines on it.
steps: Represent rules as dict: (state, symbol) -> (write, move, next_state)
Implement the run loop: look up, apply, move, repeat until halt state
Encode the binary incrementer; test on 1011, 111, 0
Encode your unary adder from lab 2; then try the 2-state busy beaver (how many 1s?)

checks.hint: Rules as a dict keyed by (state, symbol)
The busy beaver must halt — count its ones

labs.success_message: Your simulator is a universal machine in miniature — Turing's 1936 idea, running.

labs.title: The Halting Proof in Your Own Words
labs.objective: Write the impossibility proof as an essay a smart peer could follow.
steps: State the assumption clearly: suppose H decides halting for all (P, x)
Construct D: the program that does the opposite of whatever H predicts about D(D)
Derive the contradiction in plain language — no hand-waving
Close with what the proof does and doesn't imply (impossible vs hard)
labs.success_message: You now own the most important impossibility proof in computer science.

labs.title: Lambda Reduction Drills
labs.objective: Beta-reduce expressions by hand until substitution is mechanical.
steps: Reduce (λx.x) 42, (λx.λy.x) A B, (λf.λx.f x) g a
Encode TRUE/FALSE as functions; reduce (TRUE P Q) and (FALSE P Q)
Reduce (λx.x x)(λy.y) — watch self-application work
Write one paragraph: what computation IS in lambda calculus
labs.success_message: Computation without machines — functions all the way down.

labs.title: Reduction Proof Exercise
labs.objective: Prove a new language undecidable by reduction from HALT.
steps: Target: L = {P : P outputs the string 'hello'}
Assume decider A for L; construct Q(P,x): run P(x), then output 'hello'
Show A(Q) decides HALT — spell out both directions
Write the full proof; then try L2 = {P : P halts on ALL inputs}

checks.hint: The assumed decider is shown impossible

labs.success_message: You can now wield reductions — the standard weapon of undecidability.

labs.title: Paper Enigma Rotor Model
labs.objective: Build a working paper Enigma (single rotor) and encrypt a message.
steps: Draw two alphabets: outer ring (fixed) and inner rotor (rotatable), with a simple substitution
Add the reflector rule: encryption must avoid fixed points (no letter to itself)
Encrypt WETTER with rotor at position A, stepping each letter; record output
Decrypt by resetting to A and running the cipher back through — verify round-trip

checks.hint: Same settings decrypt what they encrypt

labs.success_message: You've operated Enigma's core mechanism — and felt why procedure mattered more than wiring.

labs.title: Bombe Logic Walkthrough
labs.objective: Work a crib-loop consistency check by hand, Bombe-style.
steps: Take crib WETTER -> cipher ETJRR; write the plugboard pairings as a chain
Find a loop in the chain (a letter reachable back to itself through pairings)
Assume a plugboard guess; propagate around the loop — check consistency
Show how one inconsistent loop kills a whole rotor position without testing it fully

checks.hint: One broken loop kills the position

labs.success_message: You just did what the Bombe did — constraint propagation, by hand.

labs.title: Run an Imitation Game
labs.objective: Design and run a small imitation game with proper controls.
steps: Write the protocol: players, text-only channel, time limit, human baseline, scoring rule
Run 3+ rounds: one with a human, one with a chatbot, judge blind
Record misidentification rates for BOTH human and machine
Write up: what the controls revealed that a casual chat wouldn't

checks.hint: Written protocol with controls before running

labs.success_message: You ran Turing's experiment — and learned why the controls are the science.

labs.title: Colossus Research Write-Up
labs.objective: Research and write up what Colossus was — and wasn't.
steps: Research: purpose (Tunny/Lorenz), builder (Tommy Flowers), method (statistical, electronic)
Distinguish from Bombe (Enigma keys) and from general-purpose computers
Note the secrecy: destroyed, unacknowledged for decades — cost to computing history
Deliver: 2-page brief with sources, separating documented fact from lore

checks.hint: Secrecy cost addressed with cited sources

labs.success_message: You can now tell Colossus's story accurately — a rarer skill than it should be.

labs.title: One-Time Pad by Hand
labs.objective: Encrypt and decrypt with a one-time pad; then confront the key problem.
steps: Agree on a random key as long as the message (use a coin/dice — feel the cost)
Encrypt HELLO with modular addition (A=0...Z=25); show the cipher
Decrypt with the same key; verify round-trip
Write the honest assessment: perfect secrecy, impossible key distribution — when would you actually use it?
labs.success_message: Perfect secrecy in your hands — and the reason nobody uses it.

labs.title: Gödel Explainer
labs.objective: Write the incompleteness argument for a smart non-mathematician.
steps: Explain formal systems (axioms + rules) in plain language, no jargon
Present the Gödel sentence: 'this statement is unprovable here' — and why it's true
Show the dilemma: prove it (inconsistent) or can't (incomplete)
Close with what it does and doesn't imply — defuse the mysticism

checks.hint: Both horns of the dilemma and honest limits

labs.success_message: If you can explain Gödel plainly, you understand him.

labs.title: Turing Award Laureate Study
labs.objective: Pick one Turing Award laureate and connect their work to Turing's ideas.
steps: Choose a laureate (start from the ACM list); read their citation
Summarize their core contribution in one paragraph
Draw the explicit line to Turing: which of his ideas does it extend, apply, or answer?
Present as a 5-minute talk outline

checks.hint: Explicit connection to Turing's work drawn

labs.success_message: You can now read computing's history through its highest honor.

labs.title: Reaction-Diffusion Simulation
labs.objective: Simulate Turing patterns in Python and watch spots emerge.
steps: Implement the Gray-Scott model (two chemicals, U and V, with feed/kill rates)
Run on a small grid; visualize U over time
Tune feed/kill to find spots, stripes, and chaos regimes
Write up: what the parameters do, in activator/inhibitor language

checks.hint: At least two pattern regimes found

labs.success_message: Spots from nowhere — on your screen, from Turing's 1952 equations.

labs.title: ACE Design Analysis
labs.objective: Read excerpts of Turing's 1945 ACE report and analyze the design.
steps: Find the ACE report excerpts (NPL archives / published sources)
Identify: instruction set philosophy, subroutine treatment, memory organization
Compare with a modern RISC design doc — list the echoes
Write a 2-page analysis: what was visionary, what was constrained by 1945
labs.success_message: You read a founding computer design document like an architect.

labs.title: Verified Turing Timeline
labs.objective: Build a date-verified timeline of Turing's life and work.
steps: Collect events: 1912, 1936 paper, 1939 Bletchley, 1945 ACE, 1950 paper, 1952 paper + prosecution, 1954, 2009/2013/2017
Verify each date against at least two sources (Hodges, ACM, Bletchley archives)
Note one common error per era (e.g., 'built Colossus', 'broke Enigma alone')
Deliver the timeline with sources — a reference you'd trust

checks.hint: Each date verified against two sources

labs.success_message: You now own the verified chronology — myth-resistant.

labs.title: Legacy Reflection Essay
labs.objective: Write the essay: which Turing idea matters most, and why.
steps: Choose ONE idea (UTM, undecidability, imitation game, morphogenesis, statistical crypto...)
Argue its importance: what exists because of it, what would differ without it
Steelman the case for a RIVAL idea being more important — then answer it
Close with what the idea demands of you, personally
labs.success_message: You thought with Turing's ideas, not just about them.

labs.title: Modern AI Evaluation Rubric
labs.objective: Design an evaluation rubric for a modern AI system, post-imitation-game.
steps: Define the construct: what capability are you actually measuring?
Specify: held-out data, baselines (human + trivial), adversarial cases, failure analysis
Include what the rubric CANNOT measure (Turing's honesty about limits)
Apply it to one real system or benchmark; report the gaps

checks.hint: The rubric's own limits stated; applied once

labs.success_message: You evaluate AI the way Turing taught: operationally, honestly, with limits stated.

simulations.title: The Bombe menu
simulations.brief: Three cribs for today's Enigma key. Choose the menu the Bombe should try first — and say why.

steps.symptom: Three cribs are available. The Bombe tries menus derived from cribs; closures do the logical work.
options: Run crib C first — closures do the logical work; a short crib with many closures beats a long one with few
steps.explain: The Bombe's speed comes from the menu's loop closures, which propagate contradictions. Turing's insight: the structure of the crib matters more than its length.

steps.symptom: Menu chosen. The Bombe stops — but on a false stop. What distinguishes a true stop?
options: Test the implied plugboard settings against the full crib — a true stop decodes the whole crib consistently
steps.explain: A stop is a hypothesis: the plugboard pairs it implies must decode the entire crib. False stops collapse under that check; true ones survive.

steps.symptom: Key recovered for the day. The historian asks what Turing actually automated.
evidence: hand methods: several codebreakers, hours per key
options: The systematic elimination of impossible plugboard settings — mechanized proof by contradiction at electrical speed
steps.explain: The Bombe mechanized reductio ad absurdum: assume a plugboard pairing, propagate, contradiction kills it. Turing turned logic into machinery.

simulations.debrief: The Bombe is logic made physical: cribs become menus, menus become contradictions, and contradictions eliminate keys.

simulations.title: The halting argument
simulations.brief: A manager requests a program that decides halting for all programs. Take the meeting — and the proof.

steps.symptom: The spec: H(P, I) returns True iff program P halts on input I. Do you take the contract?
evidence: H(P, I) returns True iff P halts on I
options: Decline — no such program can exist, and the proof is six lines
Accept; it is just hard engineering
steps.explain: The halting problem is undecidable — proven, not merely difficult. Taking the contract means promising the impossible.

evidence: D(P): if H(P, P) then loop forever else halt
options: Run D on itself: H(D, D) is wrong in both cases — if it says halts, D loops; if it says loops, D halts
steps.explain: Diagonalization: D does the opposite of whatever H predicts about D. Both answers are wrong, so H cannot exist.

steps.symptom: What does this mean for real tools — linters, verifiers, antivirus?
options: Perfect program analysis is impossible in general — tools approximate, bound, or restrict the language
Tools will solve it with AI
steps.explain: Undecidability draws the boundary: every analyzer is sound-but-incomplete, complete-but-unsound, or restricted. The proof tells you which corners are cut.

simulations.debrief: The halting proof is diagonalization in six lines — and it sets the boundary every program-analysis tool lives inside.

simulations.title: Design the imitation game
simulations.brief: Run a fair Turing test of a chatbot. Design the controls, interpret the result, and modernize the method.

steps.symptom: You must run a fair Turing test of a chatbot. Design the controls.
evidence: judge chats via text with a human and a machine
options: Blind the judge, limit the channel to text, and fix the time — the test measures indistinguishability under controlled conditions
Let the judge see both terminals
Tell the judge which is which
steps.explain: Turing's 1950 setup isolates the variable under test: conversational behavior. Every unblinded cue is a confound.

steps.symptom: The bot passes. A colleague claims it therefore 'thinks'. Your response?
options: Passing measures imitation under these conditions — it does not settle what thinking is; Searle's Chinese room makes the same point
steps.explain: The test is behavioral and operational. Turing offered it as a replacement for the vague question, not as a metaphysical detector.

options: Adversarial, multi-turn, task-grounded evaluation with held-out tasks — static Q&A saturates; agentic benchmarks probe deeper
steps.explain: The imitation game's spirit survives in evals: blinded, task-grounded, adversarial. The form evolves; the methodology — controlled indistinguishability — does not.

simulations.debrief: The Turing test is experimental design: blind the judge, control the channel, and remember it measures imitation, not mind.

simulations.title: Morphogenesis parameters
simulations.brief: Replicate Turing's 1952 reaction-diffusion patterns. Two chemicals, one gray screen — tune it until it spots.

steps.symptom: Two chemicals: activator and inhibitor. Nothing patterns — uniform gray.
options: Make the inhibitor diffuse much faster than the activator — differential diffusion is the pattern engine
steps.explain: Turing's condition: local activation plus long-range inhibition. Equal diffusion gives uniform mush; the ratio creates spots and stripes.

steps.symptom: Spots appear. Now they drift and merge into blobs.
options: Tune the reaction kinetics against the diffusion scale — pattern wavelength is set by their ratio
steps.explain: The ratio of reaction rate to diffusion sets the wavelength. Patterns are a balance; push one side and the pattern coarsens.

steps.symptom: Stable leopard spots. Why did this matter to biology?
options: It showed complex biological pattern needs no blueprint — local rules + diffusion generate global order
steps.explain: Morphogenesis was Turing's answer to 'where does pattern come from': emergence from simple coupled rules, no architect required.

simulations.debrief: Turing patterns are emergence made visible: differential diffusion turns uniform chemicals into spots, stripes, and shells.

simulations.title: The universal machine
simulations.brief: Why was the universal Turing machine a bigger idea than any single machine? Trace it from 1936 to the modern stack.

steps.symptom: Why was the universal Turing machine a bigger idea than any single machine?
options: One machine that reads any machine's description and runs it — software separated from hardware, the stored-program concept
steps.explain: Universality: the machine's behavior comes from the tape, not the wiring. That is the entire idea of general-purpose computing.

steps.symptom: Connect it to the modern stack.
options: Every interpreter, VM, and CPU is a universal machine in practice — code as data, executed by a fixed engine
steps.explain: An interpreter is literally a universal machine: fixed engine, program on the 'tape'. Python running Python is Turing's 1936 idea at work.

options: Interpretation overhead — universality trades raw speed for generality, which is why we compile hot paths
steps.explain: The universal machine is an interpreter, and interpretation costs. JITs and compilers are the engineering answer to Turing's tradeoff.

simulations.debrief: Universality is the stored-program idea: one fixed machine, infinite behaviors — and the interpretation overhead we have managed ever since.

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques

Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.

Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.

24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
